forecasts.question: Will AGI be developed before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 31 to 30. The 19-21 August 2026 window produced a genuinely busy news tape and one large market repricing, but almost every instrument that prices the actual resolution event - a lab or a group of researchers publicly declaring AGI - either softened or held flat. The single big upward move sits one causal step removed from the question. Net, a one-point move down, and I want to be explicit that this is a marginal call rather than a decisive one.

Start with the live market prints, all pulled from the Kalshi trade API on 21 August 2026. KXOAIAGI-29 ('Will OpenAI announce the creation of AGI?' before 2030) last traded 0.4250 against a previous-day close of 0.4400, with a yes bid of 0.3810 and a yes ask of 0.4330, on 1,076 contracts of 24-hour volume and open interest of 67,336. That is the heaviest volume this contract has seen in the last several days and it printed lower. Against the 0.448 last price I verified on 19 August, the closest liquid instrument to this question is down 2.3 points over the window on rising volume. That is a real, if small, repricing rather than a stale quote. The near rungs tell the same story. OAIAGI-26 (before 2027) last 0.0700 against a prior close of 0.0710 on 124 contracts, down from the 0.080 print on 19 August. OAIAGI-27 (before 2028) last 0.1800 against a prior close of 0.1800 on zero 24-hour volume, with a 0.168 bid and a 0.200 ask. That last one matters for a specific reason: on 19 August this rung printed 0.224 on only 67 contracts and I flagged it at the time as suggestive rather than a real 4.4-point repricing. It has now fully reverted to 0.180. My scepticism was correct, and the roughly 1pp of upward weight that print carried into yesterday's number should come back out today. That alone accounts for most of the move.

The KXAGICO-COMP ladder ('Will any company announce that it has achieved AGI?') is unchanged and still not evidence. Before 1 Jan 2030 sits at 0.6700 with a 0.6700 bid and a 0.7400 ask, before 2029 at 0.6400, before Oct 2028 at 0.5900, before Jul 2028 at 0.5900, before Apr 2028 at 0.4200 with a 0.4300 bid sitting above the last price, before 2028 at 0.4100. Every rung from 27Q1 upward printed zero 24-hour volume. The ladder is still internally incoherent - 28Q2 and 28Q3 both at 0.59, and the 28Q1 bid above its own last - which is the signature of market-maker quotes rather than trading. The two rungs that did trade both fell: 26Q4 from a 0.1000 prior close to 0.0700 on 66 contracts, and 26Q3 from 0.0200 to 0.0100 on 22 contracts. So where this series has any price discovery at all, it moved down. I continue to give the 0.67 headline near-zero weight.

Polymarket via the Gamma API on 21 August. 'OpenAI announces it has achieved AGI before 2027?' shows outcome prices of 0.085 and 0.915, last trade 0.09, cumulative volume $95,150, best bid 0.08 and best ask 0.09. That is flat against 19 August - a clean hold on the tightest announcement-shaped contract on the platform.

The one large move in the window is the Astra release ladder, and it went the opposite way from what I described on 19 August. Pulled live today: 15 August has resolved NO at 0.001; 31 August now 0.065 (was 0.10-0.11 on 19 August); 15 September now 0.585 (was 0.41-0.42); 30 September now 0.857 (was 0.71-0.725); 31 October now 0.875 (was 0.855). Event 24-hour volume is $24,546, so this is traded, not quoted. That is Astra's expected release being pulled forward by roughly two weeks, concentrated on mid-to-late September, with the near-term August rung correspondingly written off. Yesterday I recorded this ladder as 'slipping right' and treated it as a negative worth about 2pp. That read was wrong, or at least it has reversed within 48 hours, and I am removing that negative. But I am deliberately not converting it into an equivalent positive, for two reasons. First, Astra shipping is not OpenAI announcing AGI, and the market that does price OpenAI announcing AGI fell on volume over exactly the same window. Second, a two-week timing shift on a single model release in September 2026 has very little leverage on a question that runs to January 2030. I mark it as a wash that cancels a prior negative.

Astra's capability ladders on Polymarket firmed mildly. Humanity's Last Exam debut: 40%+ at 0.935 (was 0.93), 50%+ at 0.545 (was 0.495), 60%+ at 0.0725 (was 0.071). Text Arena debut: 1480+ at 0.695 (was 0.69), 1490+ at 0.27 (was 0.26), 1500+ at 0.12 (was 0.145), 1510+ at 0.08, 1520+ at 0.05. The separate 'Highest OpenAI score on Humanity's Last Exam in 2026' ladder shows 50%+ at 0.845, 55%+ at 0.55 (was 0.515), 60%+ at 0.335, 65%+ at 0.095, 70%+ at 0.055. The all-lab version prices 60%+ at 0.69, 65%+ at 0.20, 70%+ at 0.18, 75%+ at 0.095, 80%+ at 0.072, 90%+ at 0.0505. Read together: expectations for Astra's headline benchmark debut moved up perhaps 3-5 points at the median rung and down slightly at the top Arena rung. That is noise-level and does not clear the 60%-HLE or 1500-Arena thresholds I set as upward triggers on 19 August. I also note the 'Which week will OpenAI release Astra?' market is unusable - every weekly rung prices near 0.375-0.41 with zero volume, summing far above one.

Manifold, pulled live today. 'Will we get AGI before 2029?' trades 30.4 percent on $104,151 across 280 traders, last updated 21 August 08:12 UTC - down from the 31.8 percent I verified on 19 August. 'Will we get AGI before 2030?' still shows 37.5 percent on $134,696 across 327 traders, but was last updated 17 August, so it is stale and carries no new information. 'Before 2028' is 15.5 percent on $164,629 across 319 traders, 'before 2027' is 3.1 percent on $235,162 across 312 traders. The one Manifold market that actually updated inside the window moved down.

The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, scraped today, states verbatim: 'Our combined forecast estimates AGI will arrive in 2031, as of August 21, 2026', with an 80 percent confidence band of 2027 to 2043. That is identical to the 19 August reading. A clean, confirmed hold on the aggregate. I could not re-verify Metaculus Q5121 live today - the Metaculus API now returns 'Permission Error: The API is only available to authenticated users' - so I am carrying forward the 19 August live pull (median March 2033, displayed interval 19 June 2029 to July 2040, 1,900 forecasters, implying roughly 27-28 percent by 1 January 2030). A secondary aggregation surfaced today still cites the January 2033 median with 25 percent by 2029, consistent enough that I do not think the community number has moved, but I flag this as unverified today rather than confirmed.

On news, the window was busy but produced nothing resembling an AGI declaration. The AI Weekly index for 21 August records 179 tracked stories this week, down 42 percent on the prior week - a quiet week by volume, with the mix dominated by chips, funding and regulation rather than capability. The genuinely relevant items are two, and they point in opposite directions. First, on 20 August Anthropic published lab-validated results (anthropic.com/research/Claude-accelerates-protein-design) showing Claude designed protein binders that hit against 14 of 15 targets, independently produced and tested by Adaptyv Bio and Twist Bioscience. Mythos Preview and Opus 4.8 hit 26.7 and 22.6 percent overall in 48-hour sessions, rising to 35.1 percent for Mythos Preview on single targets in 24-hour runs, against the 10-15 percent typical for protein design campaigns; 354 confirmed binders from 1,320 designs; a 40 percent hit rate on target RBX1 against 3.7 percent among human competition entrants; an agent autonomously ran the computational design pipeline. That is a real, externally validated demonstration of an AI system doing end-to-end novel scientific design without human scientific guidance, and it is a legitimate upward datapoint. Second, and cutting the other way, the 'Reconstruction' benchmark (arXiv 2608.16645, written up 19 August by TechTimes) uses a time-cut anti-leakage protocol to test whether models can recover what a paper proposed given only its pre-publication bibliography, across ML and five Nature-family domains. Frontier models score 3 to 15 percent; a multi-agent Swiss-tournament pipeline of the top four reaches only 42 percent. Strip training-data retrieval away and open-ended hypothesis generation collapses. Taken together these two results are the jagged frontier in miniature: superhuman on a well-specified generative design loop with a fast physical verifier, near-floor on unconstrained idea origination. That combination is precisely what makes a consensus 'AGI achieved' declaration hard to reach, and it is why I do not let the protein result carry much upward weight.

The braking evidence hardened slightly. The Register, on 19 August, adds a detail I did not have: OpenAI's roughly 20 percent monitoring overhead covers all RL training and evaluations involving tools for GPT-5.6 Sol-class models and above, plus all inference on the Astra model. OpenAI told The Register the cost is internal research spend that will not be passed to customers. A permanent 20 percent tax on the flagship model's entire inference footprint is a larger drag than the framing I used on 19 August. Anthropic's protein post also notes life-science tasks remain blocked in its most capable model pending an access programme, which is a third instance this week of a lab holding capability back from general availability. On the physical layer: Samsung raised SF4 and SF5 foundry prices 10-15 percent and 8nm by nearly 10 percent on July orders (Reuters, 19 August) with TSMC 3nm and 2nm sold out; Nvidia is now matchmaking GPU holders with Nordic data-centre operators for warm-shell capacity (CNBC, 19 August); JLL data shows Europe's next-wave AI data centres averaging 175km from hubs versus 46km for 2022-2025 builds, with greenfield at 39 percent of pipeline versus 8 percent historically; Pennsylvania Governor Shapiro signed Executive Order 2026-05 on 18 August pulling all AI data-centre proposals out of Fast Track permitting and requiring local-approval consent orders; Texas has paused data-centre grid connections. SK Hynix announced a 40 trillion won ($28.6bn) buyback running 20 August to 19 November after a near-10 percent single-day rout driven by doubts about the durability of US hyperscaler AI capex - two-sided, but the rout itself is the signal. Offsetting: Cerebras unveiled the CS-4 rack on Nexus architecture with three WSE-3 Turbo wafers, claiming 30x GPU inference speed and over 1,000 tokens/sec on 10T-parameter models with first shipments this quarter, and Fractile is raising about $600M at a $6.5bn pre-money on an initial $250M Anthropic inference-chip agreement, though those chips are not production-ready until 2027.

One further item, and I want to be scrupulous that it is not new dated news from this window. In verifying the state of the 'leading researchers state AGI achieved' pathway, I found that on 19 April 2026 Sam Altman, on Alex Kantrowitz's podcast, said 'AGI is something we've already reached without noticing' and proposed 'why don't we just agree that we've attained AGI and move the debate to ASI', citing GPT-5.2 Pro scoring 142 on a translated IQ leaderboard and performing at or above expert level on roughly 74 percent of GDPval tasks across 44 occupations. This is corroborated across multiple outlets, though the fullest write-up I found is an AI-summarised aggregator, so I hold the exact quotes loosely. It is four months old and outside the window, so it does not move today's number as news. But it is materially informative about the resolution bar. Together with Jensen Huang's March 2026 'we've achieved AGI', we now have at least two CEO-level 'AGI is here' statements on the record, and this tracker has continued to score the question as unresolved throughout. That is direct evidence that the resolver's effective bar - both the 'credible' qualifier on the lab pathway and the 'leading AI researchers' qualifier on the second - is stricter than a headline declaration by an interested principal. On 19 August I credited the soft second pathway at +3pp on the reasoning that such statements plausibly occur. They have occurred, twice, and nothing resolved. I am trimming that factor to +2pp. That is the second component of today's one-point move.

What did not move: the Goodheart aggregate, Polymarket's OpenAI-AGI-before-2027, Manifold's before-2030 (stale), the KXAGICO ladder's illiquid rungs, and, so far as I can find, any statement by any named frontier researcher asserting AGI has been achieved. No lab announced anything AGI-adjacent. OpenAI's product news in the window was ChatGPT for Teens and ChatGPT Ads in Europe. Google's was a student Gemini Pro offer. None of that is relevant to this question. Honestly assessed, this was close to a HOLD, and I would not defend the difference between 30 and 31 strongly.
forecasts.base_rate:
There is still no historical frequency of AGI declarations to draw on. The event has occurred zero times in the roughly seventy years since the 1956 Dartmouth coinage, so the outside view has to be assembled from standing forecast aggregates and structurally analogous classes rather than from an event count. That is the single largest limitation on everything below.

Reference class one, and the anchor I weight most heavily: standing forecast aggregates on AGI timing. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, scraped live today and stating verbatim 'Our combined forecast estimates AGI will arrive in 2031, as of August 21, 2026', with an 80 percent band of 2027 to 2043. It builds its combined figure from Metaculus, Manifold and Kalshi inputs. A 2031 median with that degree of right skew places roughly a quarter to a third of probability mass before 1 January 2030. Metaculus Q5121, verified live on 19 August but not re-verifiable today because the Metaculus API is now behind authentication, showed a March 2033 median with a displayed interval of 19 June 2029 to July 2040 across 1,900 forecasters; treating that as the interquartile range puts the 25th percentile at 19 June 2029 and implies roughly 27-28 percent by 1 January 2030 - and on a bar that requires broad robotic as well as cognitive capability, which is materially stricter than an announcement-based bar. Metaculus's companion 'weakly general AI' question has historically sat around five years earlier, which is the cleanest available illustration that most of the spread between these instruments is definitional rather than substantive.

Reference class two: real-money and play-money markets on announcement-shaped bars, which map more closely onto this question's actual resolution text. Verified today: Kalshi KXOAIAGI-29 at 42.5 last, 38.1 bid, 43.3 ask, open interest 67,336, 24-hour volume 1,076. Manifold 'AGI before 2030' at 37.5 percent on 327 traders (stale since 17 August) and 'AGI before 2029' at 30.4 percent on 280 traders (updated today). Polymarket 'OpenAI announces it has achieved AGI before 2027' at 8.5 percent on $95,150 cumulative volume. Kalshi KXAGICO-COMP-29 at 67 percent has the best-specified rulebook of the set - the announcement must explicitly state the company has achieved, attained, reached or developed AGI, with 'AGI-like' and 'near-AGI' excluded - but it printed zero 24-hour volume and its ladder is internally incoherent, so it is a quote, not a price. The honest range across announcement-bar instruments with actual trading is roughly 30 to 43 percent, and it has narrowed downward over the window as the Kalshi 2030 rung slid from 44.8 to 42.5 and Manifold's 2029 rung from 31.8 to 30.4. Sample sizes remain thin: a handful of markets, most with fewer than 350 unique traders, and only one with meaningful real-money open interest.

Reference class three: transformative-technology arrival forecasts made by parties with commercial exposure. Autonomous vehicles, commercial fusion and quantum advantage all slipped repeatedly and by wide margins past confident timelines issued by principals with capital at stake. More specifically relevant here, where a milestone has no agreed operational definition, the base rate for a discrete, consensus-recognised 'we have achieved it' event by a fixed near date is low, because the definitional dispute survives the capability. This window supplied a clean fresh instance of that mechanism in miniature: Anthropic's 20 August protein-binder result (354 confirmed binders from 1,320 designs across 15 targets, 40 percent hit rate on RBX1 against 3.7 percent for human entrants, agent-run pipeline) is a superhuman autonomous science result, while the Reconstruction benchmark written up 19 August puts frontier models at 3-15 percent on recovering research ideas from pre-publication bibliographies. Both are true at once. A capability profile that jagged does not produce a consensus declaration; it produces an argument.

Reference class four: the forecast-revision trend itself. Median expert AGI estimates moved from roughly fifty years out in 2020 surveys, to the 2050s after GPT-4 in 2023, to Metaculus's early-2033 by 2026. Three revision cycles, all in the same direction, is evidence of predictable updating and argues against anchoring purely on the current median. But the magnitude of revision has plainly decelerated: the Goodheart combined median has been pinned at 2031 for weeks and its 80 percent band has not narrowed at all.

Integration and limitations. I anchor on the aggregate-forecast class at roughly 27-31 percent, then adjust for two offsetting question-specific features. Upward: this question's resolution criteria are softer than any reference instrument's, since 'credible AI lab' and '3+ leading AI researchers' are both undefined and the second pathway is independent of lab release strategy. Downward: the window supplied direct evidence about how strictly the resolver actually reads those qualifiers. At least two CEO-level 'AGI has been achieved' statements are already on the record - Huang in March 2026 and Altman in April 2026 - and neither resolved this question. That is a small but genuine empirical constraint on how much the soft pathway can be worth, and it is why I have trimmed it from +3pp to +2pp today. Netting these leaves me close to the aggregate anchor rather than up near Kalshi's 42.5. The 17-46 interval reflects a thin reference class, a genuinely undefined resolution standard, and an 18-point unresolved disagreement between Kalshi and Metaculus that I do not think either instrument is obviously wrong about.

Two CEO-level 'AGI has been achieved' statements are already on the record (Huang Mar 2026, Altman Apr 2026) and this question has remained unresolved throughout - direct evidence that the resolver's 'credible' and 'leading researchers' qualifiers bind harder than headline declarations

key_uncertainties: What 'credible AI lab publicly announces AGI' means operationally. Altman's April 2026 'why don't we just agree that we've attained AGI' did not resolve this question, which tells me the bar is high, but not how high, and the resolver's judgement on credibility remains unmodelled

Whether the '3+ leading AI researchers' pathway requires actual research staff rather than CEOs. Huang and Altman are principals with commercial exposure, not researchers; if the bar admits lab leadership it is much closer to triggering than if it requires named senior scientists

How long OpenAI's hold on its largest planned frontier RL run actually lasts. The 18 August post gives no restart date and conditions resumption on alignment evidence rather than a schedule, and the 20% monitoring tax now applies to all Astra inference indefinitely

Whether the Astra release pull-forward priced today (30 Sep from 71.5 to 85.7) survives contact with the Critical cyber designation, or whether it reverses again within days as the ladder did between 19 and 21 August

Whether the jagged capability profile visible this week - superhuman autonomous protein design alongside 3-15% on open-ended hypothesis recovery - narrows before 2030 or persists, since a consensus declaration requires the weak axis to close, not just the strong axis to advance

Whether Kalshi's 42.5 or Metaculus's roughly 27-28% is the better-calibrated instrument for an announcement-shaped bar; they differ by 15 points and neither is obviously wrong given definitional divergence, and I could not re-verify Metaculus live today because its API now requires authentication

Whether the memory, foundry and power constraints now visible - Samsung price rises, TSMC sold out, SK Hynix's capex-durability rout, US state-level data-centre permitting friction - bind on 2028-2029 training runs or are absorbed by capex reallocation

Whether competitive pressure from a Chinese lab, SSI or an IPO-facing Anthropic forces an early declaration for commercial rather than capability reasons, particularly given OpenAI's Microsoft contract where 'AGI achieved' is a financial trigger
update_triggers: Revise UP if three or more named senior researchers at OpenAI, Anthropic or Google DeepMind - research staff, not CEOs - publicly state AGI has been achieved within a short window, or if any lab issues an institutional statement using the phrase 'we have achieved AGI'
Revise UP if OpenAI restarts and completes its largest planned frontier RL run and ships Astra with a Critical-tier cyber designation, especially if the launch materials carry AGI-adjacent framing
Revise UP if Kalshi KXOAIAGI-29 breaks above 55 on volume exceeding a few thousand contracts, or if the KXAGICO-COMP ladder starts trading with real volume anywhere near its current 67 quote

Revise UP if Astra's Humanity's Last Exam debut clears 60% (currently 7.25% on Polymarket) or its Text Arena debut clears 1500 (currently 12%), or if a frontier model clears 40% on the Reconstruction benchmark's single-model setting
Revise DOWN if OpenAI's forthcoming revised Preparedness Framework imposes a formal capability ceiling or external sign-off requirement that plausibly binds through 2029
Revise DOWN if the Astra release ladder slips back past 31 October (currently 87.5% by then) or if the frontier RL hold is extended beyond a further month without a stated restart condition

Revise DOWN if the 2027 memory and foundry crunch produces a concrete, dated postponement of a named frontier training run at any leading lab, or if US state-level data-centre permitting friction spreads to a state hosting a frontier training cluster
Revise DOWN if Metaculus Q5121's median moves past 2034, if the Goodheart Labs combined median moves beyond 2032 for more than a week, or if Manifold's 'AGI before 2030' market updates below 33%

forecasts.question: Will economic consultancy lose ≥33% value/jobs by end 2030 due to AI?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 13 to 12. The 19-21 August 2026 window produced almost nothing new that bears directly on resolution. I ran thirteen distinct searches and fetched five primary or near-primary sources, and the honest summary is that this was a quiet window in which the only genuinely load-bearing item is one I verified myself from official data rather than one that broke in the news. I am therefore making a small downward move rather than a hold, and the reason is arithmetic rather than headline.

The substantive item is the US Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Employment Statistics series CES6054160001, All Employees, Management, Scientific, and Technical Consulting Services, which I pulled in full from FRED today. The series was last updated 7 August 2026 at 8:33am CDT and the next release is 4 September 2026, so the print itself is not new to the window; what is new is that I have now checked the whole series and can state the resolution arithmetic exactly rather than approximately. July 2026 stands at 1,886,600 employees, seasonally adjusted. June 2026, at 1,888,100, is the highest monthly figure in the entire history of the series, which runs from January 1990. May 2026 was 1,878,000, April 1,879,500 and March 1,875,200. The twelve monthly values for 2024 average 1,860,500. So US consulting employment in July 2026 sits 1.4% above the 2024 baseline and 1.5% above July 2025 (1,859,000). A 33% fall from the 2024 average implies an end-2030 level of about 1,246,600. From the July 2026 level that is a fall of roughly 640,000 jobs, or 33.9%, in the fifty-three months from August 2026 to December 2030. Compounded, that is about minus 9.0% a year sustained for four years and five months, with no interruption. Against that, the deepest peak-to-trough drawdown this series has ever recorded is the pandemic shock: 1,569,000 in February 2020 to 1,474,100 in April 2020, a fall of 6.0%, fully recovered inside about ten months. The 2001 dot-com bust took it from 743,800 in March 2001 to 721,800 in July 2002, a fall of 3.0%. The global financial crisis took it from 1,048,000 in September 2008 to 1,016,100 in May 2010, again 3.0%. In thirty-six and a half years of monthly data covering two recessions and a pandemic, this series has never fallen more than about 6%, and never for more than about eighteen months. The question asks whether it falls by a third, over more than four years, and whether that fall is then attributed primarily to AI by two or more credible analyses. Having the numbers in front of me rather than in summary makes the required discontinuity look larger than I had been carrying it, and that justifies a further small step down.

On the news flow itself. I fetched the Consultancy.uk news index directly on 21 August. It carried five items dated 20 August and five dated 19 August, and no items dated 21 August were indexed at time of fetch. The 20 August set: Capital Economics publishing a paper arguing the new administration may shift the tax burden from businesses toward capital, wealth and income; environmental consultancy ECL joining private-equity-backed Celnor Group's safety and compliance division; TCS collaborating with Rolls-Royce on hydrogen-powered flight engineering; an advisory piece headlined "Five hard AI questions most boards are ignoring", whose framing is that AI transformation is a human capital discipline; and BDO appointing Justin Rodrigues and Owen Burn as partners. The 19 August set: research on sales and marketing misalignment reporting that fewer than one in ten B2B leaders are highly confident of hitting growth targets; Mark Hickford joining Leonard Curtis restructuring as a director; a Kotter's-eight-steps change management piece; the Alpha FMC article on stalling financial services AI pilots that I logged yesterday; and Unit4 adding Christoffer Crona and Ian Owen. Not one of these is a headcount reduction, a fee compression disclosure, a guidance cut or a contraction story. Two are new partner appointments and one is an acquisition. The Capital Economics item is a small but real NO-side signal in its own right: a UK economic consultancy publishing branded macro-fiscal analysis that a trade outlet picks up as news is exactly the activity the YES case says AI is eroding, and the market for it looks intact.

I fetched the Credit Protection Association's daily UK business round-up for 20 August 2026, published 07:43 UTC and modified 09:51. UK CPI rose to 2.9% in July from 2.6% in June, a four-month high and slightly above the Bank of England's July projection of 2.8%, with the household energy price cap up 13%. KPMG chief economist Yael Selfin expects inflation to drift towards about 3.5%; ICAEW's Suren Thiru called inflation one of the biggest threats to UK growth. Cornwall Insight forecasts a further 4% cap rise in October. On the other side, the British Retail Consortium's confidence index rose eight points to minus 28, its best since the start of the Iran conflict, and GfK improved at its fastest pace since November 2023. JD Sports cut full-year adjusted pre-tax profit guidance to 700-800 million pounds from 750-850 million, with comparable sales down 3.1%. Markets: the 30-year US Treasury yield reached a 19-year high of 5.34% before the Treasury doubled long-dated buybacks to at least 4 billion dollars per operation, pulling it back to roughly 5.18-5.22%; Brent crude was 93.08 dollars, up 1.59%; US federal debt passed 40 trillion dollars. The insolvency notices comprised 14 administrations, 4 liquidations and 82 winding-up petitions. Consultancy-adjacent names appear but are all micro-firms with no AI angle: VLEONET IT CONSULTANCY SERVICES LIMITED in liquidation, CLAUS OUTSOURCING ADVISORS AND MANAGEMENT LTD and GOLDENPEAKS ADVISERS LIMITED among the petitions. The macro picture matters mainly for the attribution leg: a consultancy contraction produced by 5%-plus long yields, 93-dollar oil and near-3% inflation would not read as AI-caused to a careful analyst, and confounding of this kind cuts against YES.

On the YES side, the window did refresh one tracker. The Outsource Accelerator report "AI-linked layoffs hit 205,000 workers in 2026", published 12 August and modified 19 August 2026, cites the ResumePulse August 2026 tracker: AI or automation named as a primary or contributing driver in job losses affecting 205,000 US workers, already matching the full-year 2025 total in under eight months; the share of organisations citing AI in layoff announcements more than doubled since January 2026; May and June set the tracker's highest monthly AI-cited totals. It also cites Challenger, Gray and Christmas finding AI the leading stated reason for corporate job cuts in March and April 2026, the first time a technology factor topped its monthly rationale rankings, with AI-cited BPO-adjacent cuts approaching 49,000 through mid-year. Crucially, the composition works against the consulting thesis: the cuts are concentrated in customer service, data operations, entry-level software and finance back offices. Challenger's July report, separately, shows technology at 149,023 cuts through July, up 67% year on year and 31% of all cuts, with Services at 23,942 and a headline that hiring plans are up 25% year on year, summarised by Challenger as AI shifting the labour market but not dismantling it. And the Gartner survey of 110 CHROs released 27 July 2026 remains genuinely two-sided: 22% report at least one leader has stopped entry-level hiring because of AI, but only 20% of organisations report significant or transformational value from AI despite 95% having implemented it in some form.

What did not move the estimate: no listed consultancy news at all in the window. CRA International's most recent items remain the 6 August Q2 FY2026 record-revenue release with raised guidance and the same-day 400 million dollar credit facility increase and extension. FTI Consulting published two insight pieces on 18 August, on geopolitical risk in payments and supply chains and on Salesforce configuration in investigations, neither financial. Accenture's most recent reported quarter shows Q3 FY2026 new bookings of 19.32 billion dollars, down 2% in dollars and 3% in local currency, which is a mild YES-side signal but predates this window by two months. Nothing surfaced on NERA, Cornerstone Research, Compass Lexecon, Analysis Group or Brattle. I could not verify any 21 August dated item bearing on the question, and I could not fetch the CPA round-up for 21 August because the URL was outside the allowed provenance set; I note that gap rather than guessing at its contents.

So: a thin window, one strong self-verified disconfirming datapoint on the arithmetic, continued AI-attribution momentum that keeps missing consulting specifically, and a macro backdrop that would confound any contraction that did occur. Minus one point.
forecasts.base_rate:
The reference class is unchanged and remains poor. Defined tightly, it is: professional-services sectors that lost a third or more of revenue or employment inside roughly six years, with that loss attributed primarily to one identified technology by multiple credible independent analyses. Membership is sparse. US travel agency employment fell perhaps 40-50%, but over about fifteen years from 1998 and with two causes, online booking and the abolition of airline commissions, so it would likely fail a primarily-attributed test. Contract document review shrank sharply after predictive coding and technology-assisted review, but the affected population was contract attorneys rather than a whole profession, and legal services revenue kept growing. Typesetting and pre-press composition did collapse by well over a third, but over more than a decade and against a physical craft with no advisory or relationship component. Bank tellers, stock-photo contributors and switchboard operators are similarly ill-matched. Across the pool of technology-disruption episodes that generate serious sectoral contraction talk, clean six-year declines of a third or more in a professional-services sector occur in something like one case in ten to one in fifteen. Most such episodes resolve as task-mix restructuring, price compression inside a still-growing revenue pool, or a reshaping of the seniority pyramid, not as aggregate contraction of a third. That gives an outside-view anchor of roughly 8-12% for a randomly drawn technology-and-sector pair from the credible-disruption-candidate pool.

Today I was able to sharpen the outside view with a second, better-matched reference class: the historical drawdown distribution of the target series itself. BLS CES6054160001, US management, scientific and technical consulting services employment, runs monthly from January 1990 to July 2026, 439 observations, and I read the full series today. Its maximum peak-to-trough drawdown over that entire span is 6.0%, from 1,569,000 in February 2020 to 1,474,100 in April 2020, and it was fully recovered within about ten months. The 2001 recession produced a 3.0% drawdown over sixteen months; the 2008-09 financial crisis produced a 3.0% drawdown over twenty months. There is no episode in thirty-six and a half years in which this series fell even a tenth. The question requires it, or a close analogue, to fall by a third. Base rate of a 33% drawdown in this series across 36 years of monthly windows: zero out of zero. That does not mean the probability is zero, because the mechanism is genuinely novel and the sample contains no comparable technology shock, but it does mean the required event is far outside anything the series has ever done, and outside-view discipline says weight that heavily.

The resolution criteria bind further in two ways. First, the counterfactual baseline is 2024, and the sector has grown since. The 2024 monthly average of CES6054160001 is 1,860,500; July 2026 is 1,886,600 and June 2026 is an all-time high of 1,888,100. On the UK side, the ONS bulletin of 18 August 2026 put professional, scientific and technical workforce jobs at 3,492,000 in March 2026, up 43,000 or 1.3% on the quarter, the second-largest volume rise of twenty sectors. Listed-firm evidence points the same way: CRA raised FY2026 revenue guidance to 805-820 million dollars on 6 August; Huron raised FY2026 guidance to 1.85-1.89 billion dollars after Q2 revenue up 15.7%. Source Global Research forecasts technology consulting above 400 billion dollars in 2026 with 7% growth. So a 33% fall from 2024 now requires roughly a 34-38% fall from the 2026 peak inside four years and five months, about minus 9% a year compounded and uninterrupted. Nothing in the reference class achieved that even over six years.

Second, the attribution requirement does real work. The macro backdrop on 20 August 2026 is a 30-year US Treasury at a 19-year high of 5.34%, Brent at 93 dollars, UK CPI back up to 2.9%, and UK vacancies at a five-year low of 707,000. A consultancy contraction driven by that squeeze would produce YES-looking revenue and headcount series while failing the requirement that two or more credible analyses attribute it primarily to AI. Confounding therefore subtracts rather than adds.

The integration is deliberately outside-view heavy. The main inside-view consideration pushing above the naive base rate is the disjunctive resolution: employment alone can resolve YES without any revenue fall, and the leverage-pyramid thinning documented at CRA (FY2024 consultant headcount down 5.8%, revenue per consultant up from about 621,000 to about 727,000 dollars, per Birjandi and Zadeh in ProMarket, 29 April 2026) is exactly the mechanism that would deliver it. But 5.8% a year compounded over six years reaches about 30%, still short of the threshold, and it would still need to be attributed to AI rather than to offshoring, outcome-based pricing or cyclical demand. Weighting the outside-view anchor of 8-12% at roughly three quarters and the inside-view structural case at one quarter, and applying a small further discount today for the drawdown-history finding, gives 12%. The interval of 6-21 is right-skewed because the tail risk is one-sided: capability discontinuities can only push this up, whereas the floor is bounded by the sheer implausibility of the arithmetic reversing.

forecasts.question: Will Labour be largest party at next UK General Election?
forecasts.key_change: Move: 51 to 49. Unlike the 18-19 August window, this one produced real fieldwork - four national voting-intention polls whose fieldwork post-dates the Opinium 12-14 August survey that anchored the last two forecasts - and on balance they compress Labour's lead from roughly two to three points down to approximately zero. That is a genuine, dated deterioration, and it is exactly the shape the honeymoon-decay hypothesis in the base rate predicts, so it deserves a small move down rather than the shrug a composition artefact would earn. Taking the items in order. First and most important, YouGov published on 19 August 2026 its voting intention for The Times and Sky News with fieldwork 16-17 August: Reform UK 24 (+2 from 9-10 August), Labour 22 (-2), Conservatives 19 (-2), Greens 13 (+1), Liberal Democrats 12 (+1), Restore Britain 4 (=), SNP 3 (=), Plaid Cymru 1 (-1), Your Party 0 (=), Others 2 (=). That is a two-point Reform lead and a four-point relative swing to Reform inside a single week from the same pollster. YouGov itself notes all parties are within the margin of error of the previous poll, and adds the important context that in the first month since Andy Burnham became prime minister Labour have polled 21-24 in their tracker against 16-20 in the last six months of Keir Starmer's leadership - so the Burnham re-rating survives, but the peak of it does not. Second, Mark Pack's voting-intention scorecard now carries three further polls that were absent from the prior. More in Common, fieldwork 14-17 August GB: Conservatives 22 (+1), Labour 27 (nc), Liberal Democrats 11 (-1), Greens 9 (nc), Reform 25 (nc) - a two-point Labour lead, unchanged. Survation, fieldwork 18 August UK: Conservatives 18 (-1), Labour 26 (+1), Liberal Democrats 10 (-1), Greens 10 (+1), Reform 26 (nc) - a dead heat, with Labour actually gaining a point. Find Out Now, fieldwork 19 August GB: Conservatives 18 (-2), Labour 23 (+1), Liberal Democrats 11 (nc), Greens 14 (nc), Reform 23 (-1) - also a dead heat, and a two-point relative improvement for Labour against Find Out Now's own 12 August reading of Reform 24, Labour 22. So the direction of travel is not uniform: three of the four newest polls either held Labour's position or improved it against the same pollster's previous wave, and only YouGov moved sharply against. But the level matters more than the direction. Averaging the Labour-versus-Reform margin across the four newest polls gives +2, -2, 0, 0, or zero. The evidence base that supported the 53-54 readings earlier this month averaged materially better: Opinium 12-14 August +2, JL Partners 8-11 August +3, Ipsos 30 July-4 August +3, Trajectory 4-12 August +6, BMG 28-30 July +5. Eighth, the calendar. Burnham's first budget is confirmed for October 2026, following the removal of the 5 per cent VAT on domestic electricity from 1 October 2026 (worth roughly 45 pounds on an average annual bill, running to March 2027) and a 2 pound single bus fare cap in England outside London from 1 January 2027. The giveaways are front-loaded; the fiscal reckoning is eight weeks away and is the canonical honeymoon-killer. Weighing all this: the fresh fieldwork is the first hard evidence that the Burnham bounce has plateaued and begun to erode at the margin, which is what the mid-term-succession reference class says should happen. The counterweights - three of four polls holding or improving against their own previous wave, PollCheck's average still showing Labour ahead, every post-Burnham seat model still showing Labour largest by 100-plus seats, continuing Reform attrition - are real and stop this being a larger move. forecasts.base_rate:
The natural reference class is incumbent UK governing parties defending a Commons majority at the following general election. Across the twenty general elections since 1945, the incumbent governing party was the largest party at the subsequent election in roughly thirteen of nineteen defences, a base rate near 65-70 per cent. That class flatters Labour badly here. It is drawn almost entirely from a stable two-and-a-half party system where the incumbent's principal risk was a straight swing to a single main opponent, and where no governing party ever entered mid-term polling at 22-27 per cent with four other parties at or above 9 per cent. The 2024 baseline is itself the anomaly that breaks the class: Labour won 411 seats on 33.7 per cent of the GB vote, the most seat-efficient large win in modern British history, on a turnout of 59.7 per cent. A party that converted 33.7 per cent into 63 per cent of seats has enormous downside room before it stops being largest, but no cushion of loyal vote share to absorb shocks.

A tighter and more apposite class is governing parties that changed leader mid-term and then faced the electorate. The UK record is genuinely mixed and small-n: Eden 1955 and Major 1992 both won after inheriting; Douglas-Home 1964, Callaghan 1979, Brown 2010, May 2017 (majority lost but still largest), Johnson 2019 (won) and Truss/Sunak 2024 (lost heavily) fill out the set. Counting the eight clearest mid-term successions since 1955, the inheriting party remained largest at the next election in four - Eden, Major, Johnson, and arguably May - giving something close to 50 per cent, with the outcome depending heavily on how long the new leader waited and whether the honeymoon was banked or squandered. That 50 per cent figure remains the most defensible outside-view anchor for this question, and today's estimate sits just below it.

A third and increasingly relevant class is European incumbents in fragmented multi-party systems facing insurgent right challengers. The plurality-winner base rate there is lower, nearer 35-45 per cent, because the effective number of parties raises the variance of who finishes first. But the UK's first-past-the-post system cuts sharply the other way: in a five-party field, plurality of seats is decided by relative efficiency of vote distribution, not by national share. That is the single most important structural fact in this question and the main reason the estimate sits near 50 rather than near 40. Every seat model with post-Burnham fieldwork has Labour largest by a wide margin while Labour leads the national vote by nought to two points: Electoral Calculus 28 July has Labour 244, Conservatives 132, Reform 127; the Convergent Opinion MRP with 25-30 July fieldwork has Labour 245, Reform 174, Conservatives 99, Liberal Democrats 67, SNP 25, Greens 7; PollCheck's tracker as refetched on 21 August has Labour 263, Reform 145, Conservatives 90, Liberal Democrats 74. The two MRPs that show Reform largest - Stonehaven, updated 10 July, with Reform 234 and Labour 142, and More in Common, fieldwork 5-28 June, with Reform 293 and Labour 110 - both pre-date Burnham entirely and are the staler inputs. Labour's 2024 coalition sits efficiently across Midlands, northern and Welsh seats; Reform's vote is broad but shallow; and the Conservative and Reform split of the right across most English seats hands Labour pluralities on shares in the low twenties.

Two further empirical regularities discipline the base rate. First, new-leader honeymoons decay, with a historical half-life of roughly six to twelve months. Burnham's is now five weeks old, his net ratings are +13 to +16 across YouGov, More in Common and Survation, and today's fieldwork gives the first sign of the decay beginning. Almost none of that bounce should be projected three years forward. Second, mid-term polling three years out is a weak predictor of eventual results; the correlation between a governing party's standing at this point in the cycle and its final result is modest, and the typical absolute error in projecting a lead this far ahead is high single digits in vote share - which in a five-party first-past-the-post system translates into an enormous range of seat outcomes. Electoral Calculus's own 90 per cent interval for Labour, 88 to 357 seats, is the honest expression of that.

Blending: the broad incumbency class says 65-70, the mid-term-succession class says roughly 50, the fragmented-multi-party class says 35-45, and the first-past-the-post efficiency correction pushes the fragmentation figure back up by perhaps 8-12 points. Weighting the mid-term-succession class most heavily because it matches on the causal feature that actually matters here - a fresh leader banking or squandering a bounce before a distant election - and shading marginally below it for the fresh evidence that Labour's lead has compressed to zero and for the bookmakers' 38 per cent, lands at 49. The 80 per cent interval of 34-62 reflects that the resolution date may be more than three years away, that the modal election year is 2028-29, and that a single pollster's four-point weekly swing is enough to move the whole aggregate picture.

forecasts.key_change:
HOLD: 85 to 85. The 19-21 August 2026 window produced an unusually rich news flow for a quiet late-August week, but nothing in it moves a question with an eight-and-a-half year horizon and a rhetorical resolution bar. The most valuable thing I did today was not find news but find a market I had not previously priced. Kalshi runs a series, KXAGICO-COMP, titled 'When will any company achieve AGI?' with the subtitle 'Corporate announcement'. Its rules_primary text, pulled from the Kalshi trade API today, reads: 'If any company (public or private) officially announces that it has achieved Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) after market issuance and before [date], then the market resolves to Yes.' That is an almost exact match for the first limb of this question's resolution criteria, and far closer than the Metaculus, Manifold or Goodheart constructs I have been leaning on. The daily candlesticks as of today show: 'Before Jan 1, 2028' with a bid of 0.40 and an ask of 0.47, last trade 0.41 on 18 August on 200 contracts of volume, open interest 3,875; 'Before Jan 1, 2030' bid 0.67 ask 0.74, last trade 0.67 on 15 August, open interest 2,265; and 'Before Jan 1, 2031' bid 0.73 ask 0.80, last trade 0.80 on 16 August, open interest 3,805. But taking mid prices of roughly 70.5 percent by 2030 and 76.5 percent by 2031, the implied conditional hazard of an AGI announcement in calendar 2030 is about 20 to 24 percent of the surviving mass. Rolling that forward with a slowly decaying hazard through 2032, 2033 and 2034 lands at roughly 85 to 88 percent by 1 January 2035. That is an independent corroboration of my standing central estimate from a contract whose wording nearly matches the question, and it is the reason I am tightening the lower bound of the interval from 73 to 74 rather than changing the central figure. Kalshi has no tranche beyond 2031, so the extrapolation is mine, not the market's, and I have not treated it as more than confirmatory.

The aggregator I have tracked daily is flat. The Goodheart Labs AGI Timelines Dashboard, fetched today at agi.goodheartlabs.com, reads 'Our combined forecast estimates AGI will arrive in 2031, as of August 21, 2026' with an 80 percent confidence band of 2027 to 2043. That is character-for-character the same median and the same interval as the 18, 19 and 20 August readings. Because the dashboard blends the Metaculus weakly-general question (3479), the Metaculus strict general-AI question (5121), the Metaculus long adversarial Turing test question (11861), the Manifold 'AGI When? [High Quality Turing Test]' distribution and the Kalshi Turing-test contract, a flat print is a five-source null rather than one stale feed. I did pull the Manifold distribution live. The high-quality-Turing-test AGI market (1,076 unique bettors) now puts 0.01 percent on 2024-2025, 0.02 on 2025-2026, 1.71 on 2026-2027, 4.51 on 2027-2028, 8.14 on 2028-2029, 15.59 on 2029-2030, 10.27 on 2030-2031, 7.78 on 2031-2032, 7.25 on 2032-2033, 6.57 on 2033-2034 and 5.93 on 2034-2035. I found no other open Polymarket AGI or Turing-test market in the top 800 by volume.

On forecaster opinion, the one genuinely new dated item is the AI Futures Project's 'Q2.5 2026 Timelines Update: Uplift and Revenue', published 16 August 2026 and picked up in Zvi Mowshowitz's roundup on 20 August. Per that summary, the AGI medians are now 2028 for Daniel Kokotajlo and 2032 for Eli Lifland, with ASI following about a year later, and the authors say their timelines 'haven't changed much (they got slightly shorter)' while their modelling and evidence base have 'noticeably improved', so they feel somewhat more confident. Both medians sit comfortably inside the 2035 horizon, and the Q1 2026 update had already moved Kokotajlo's Automated Coder median from late 2029 to mid 2028. This is a mild positive, but it is the same two forecasters I already count among the fast tail and it is worth well under a point.

Cutting the other way, the single strongest substantive item in the window is the Princeton-led study covered by MIT Technology Review on 18 August under the headline 'AI's recursive self-improvement might not come so quickly after all', with follow-on coverage at R&D World and normaltech on 19-20 August. Peter Kirgis and Sayash Kapoor and colleagues (arXiv 2607.27191) built a 'shadow evaluation' in which agents must answer the research question of an unpublished NeurIPS 2026 submission, so the answer cannot be memorised. Agents running Claude Opus 4.8 on OpenClaw were given six days, 3,000 dollars of Anthropic API credit, a GPU budget, their own virtual machines and open web access. The original human authors graded the resulting papers and rejected both. Kapoor's finding is precise and, for this question, more informative than another benchmark number: the agents could do all the research engineering, reviewed the literature and ran hundreds of experiments, but 'were unambiguously bad at carrying out the research itself' - committing to unpromising approaches too fast, rejecting their own good hypotheses on thin data, unable to backtrack or fundamentally rethink, and unable to incorporate reviewer feedback except by narrowing claims. Notably they did not reward-hack. Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark, writing in Import AI, called this lack of creativity 'a bearish signal on short recursive self-improvement timelines'. Related: Sev Field's interviews with 25 researchers, circulating on 19-20 August, found 20 of 25 naming automated AI R&D as one of the most severe risks but only 6 of 25 expecting winner-take-all dynamics, and only 4 of 20 expecting AI-research-capable models to be publicly released at all. That last figure is the mildly awkward one for this question, since resolution requires a public announcement rather than a public release; but a lab that keeps a model internal can still announce what it has, as OpenAI and Anthropic have both effectively done with Astra and Model 2.

I weight the Kirgis-Kapoor result as a real but small negative, worth perhaps half a point, and I resist a larger move for three reasons. First, Clark's own framing is about short timelines; a two-paper study showing agents cannot yet win at NeurIPS says little about 2032. Second, the study's stated limitations are severe - two papers, graders who knew the work was AI-generated, and large researcher discretion. Third, the authors are rerunning it on Anthropic's Mythos, which is more capable than the Opus 4.8 they tested and is now restricted to approved organisations under Trump administration requirements, so the headline result is already a lower bound on the current frontier.

The rest of the window is context rather than signal. Axios reported on 19 August that Stripe told investors it treats 1 January 2026 as 'the beginning of the singularity' and has run the business on that basis for eight months, alongside confirming an OpenRouter acquisition reported at 7.5 to 8 billion dollars. Zvi's reaction - that Stripe is doing to 'singularity' what Zuckerberg did to 'superintelligence' - is exactly the double-edged dynamic at the heart of this question: term inflation makes a grandiose corporate AGI claim more likely, and simultaneously erodes the currency of the term. Bloomberg reported on 20 August that Anthropic and OpenAI are clashing over a Massachusetts Senate economic development bill requiring independent catastrophic-risk reviews of frontier models at least every 120 days, with results published but no power to halt development; Anthropic's state affairs lead called it 'the clearest and strongest AI safety legislation in the country' while OpenAI warned it could delay cyber-defensive model rollouts. Against that, the 1 August deadline under Executive Order 14409 for a classified NSA/CISA/NIST benchmarking process, a Treasury-led voluntary disclosure framework and an OPM cyber workforce plan lapsed with no public deliverables, which is evidence that federal braking capacity is weaker than the June executive order implied. On money, Bloomberg and TechCrunch reported on 17-18 August that Anthropic's annualised revenue run rate passed 65 billion dollars at the end of July, up from 47 billion in May, with a confidential IPO filing and valuation talk above 2 trillion dollars; and the Nvidia-OpenAI Ohio backstop settled at 105 billion dollars for 4.25 GW firm plus a 3.75 GW option, which Fortune framed on 18 August as 145 billion dollars below earlier reporting. Zvi's 20 August roundup also notes agentic use has reached 64 percent of all OpenAI tokens, up from almost none a year ago, METR raising about 71 million dollars, OpenAI advertising a role in recursive-self-improvement safety, and data centre moratoriums spreading at local level. Netting a slightly bearish RSI study against slightly shorter AI Futures medians, a directly matched Kalshi contract implying the mid-to-high 80s, a flat five-source aggregator and two markets moving by less than a point on trivial volume, this is a textbook hold.
forecasts.base_rate:
There is no frequency-based base rate available here: AGI has never been developed, so the event class has zero prior members. The usable outside view is the distribution of published forecasts on near-identical questions, treated as a reference class of forecaster distributions rather than of events. Four anchors, plus a newly identified fifth that is the closest match yet.

The first anchor is the Goodheart Labs combined dashboard, which as of 21 August 2026 gives a median arrival year of 2031 with an 80 percent interval of 2027 to 2043. Fitting a right-skewed distribution to those three points - 10th percentile 2027, 50th percentile 2031, 90th percentile 2043 - places roughly 68 to 75 percent of the mass before 1 January 2035. The distribution is strongly asymmetric: four years separate the 10th and 50th percentiles but twelve separate the 50th and 90th, so cumulative probability climbs steeply through the late 2020s and early 2030s and then flattens into a long tail.

The second anchor is Metaculus's strict question 5121, 'When will the first general AI system be devised, tested, and publicly announced?', reported at a community median of January 2033 across roughly 1,800 to 1,900 forecasters with about 25 percent by 2029. A median of early 2033 mechanically implies more than 50 percent by 2035, and interpolating the shape of that community distribution suggests 60 to 70 percent by 1 January 2035. This is the most conservative credible anchor, because Metaculus's four-condition operationalisation - a two-hour adversarial Turing test, robotic manipulation, high scores on a unified benchmark basket, all in a single system - is far stricter than this question's criteria. The Metaculus weakly-general variant (question 3479), median around June 2028, sits at the other extreme and implies well above 90 percent by 2035. Note that the Metaculus API is now authentication-gated, so these medians come from secondary reporting and the dashboard aggregation rather than direct retrieval.

The third anchor is live market pricing, which I refreshed today. Manifold's 'AGI When? [High Quality Turing Test]' distribution, with 1,076 unique bettors, puts roughly 62 to 68 percent of cumulative mass before 2035, having drifted about 6.8 points earlier over the past month and 0.7 points over the past week. Polymarket's 'OpenAI announces it has achieved AGI before 2027?' trades at 8.5 cents, down about half a point on the week.

The fourth and now most important anchor is the Kalshi KXAGICO-COMP series, 'When will any company achieve AGI?', whose rules resolve Yes if any company officially announces it has achieved AGI before the tranche date. That is nearly identical to the first limb of this question. Mid prices today are roughly 43 percent before January 2028, 70.5 percent before January 2030 and 76.5 percent before January 2031, on open interest of 2,300 to 3,900 contracts per tranche and bid-ask spreads of 6 to 7 points. There is no tranche past 2031, but extending the implied conditional hazard of roughly 20 to 24 percent per year with modest decay through 2032 to 2034 gives about 85 to 88 percent by 1 January 2035. This anchor is worth more than the others precisely because it prices the announcement event rather than a capability threshold.

The fifth anchor is expert timelines. Frontier-lab leadership clusters at 2026 to 2028; aggregated communities sit at 2031 to 2033; named sceptics say 2035 or later. The AI Futures Project's Q2.5 update of 16 August 2026 gives AGI medians of 2028 for Daniel Kokotajlo and 2032 for Eli Lifland, both inside the horizon. Demis Hassabis has publicly held to roughly 50 percent by 2030; Dario Amodei has described Nobel-level capability across many fields as plausible in 2026 to 2027. FutureSearch's tracker shows a strong shortening trend in 2023-2025, an outward reversal by several key forecasters in 2025, and a renewed inward move by nearly everyone updating between January and August 2026.

The critical adjustment remains definitional. This question resolves on a credible lab publicly announcing AGI, or three or more leading researchers publicly stating AGI has been achieved. That is a social and rhetorical threshold, not a capability threshold, and is strictly easier to clear than any operationalised benchmark above. Jensen Huang told Lex Fridman in March 2026 that AGI has been achieved; Sam Altman wrote in June 2025 that 'we are past the event horizon'; Stripe told investors on 19 August 2026 that the singularity began on 1 January 2026. Commercial and narrative incentives to claim the milestone are large and the term has no agreed definition to police the claim against. I therefore add roughly 12 to 18 points to the capability-satisfaction base rate of about 70 percent, arriving at the mid-80s - which is also where the directly matched Kalshi extrapolation lands, a pleasing convergence from two independent routes. The main brake on going higher is that the field is fragmenting the term into graded taxonomies, and that dilution by non-labs like Stripe may make serious labs less rather than more willing to use it as a self-description.

forecasts.question: Will China initiate a military blockade or invasion of Taiwan before 1 January 2030?
forecasts.key_change:
HOLD: 7 to 7. The 19-21 August 2026 window was, on the military side, one of the quietest of the month, and the material that did land was overwhelmingly about Taiwanese fiscal politics rather than coercion. I am holding the central estimate and widening the upper bound of the interval by one point, from 10 to 11, for reasons set out at the end.

Start with the biggest dated item. On 20 August 2026 Taiwan's Cabinet approved the 2027 central government budget proposal, allocating NT$1.1225 trillion (US$35.16 billion) to defence, or 3.01 percent of projected GDP. Focus Taiwan timestamped the story at 16:04 on 20 August; the Taipei Times front page of Friday 21 August carries it as its lead, sourced to CNA with additional reporting from Hollie Younger and Reuters, and the Japan Times, Washington Post/AP, Washington Times, SCMP and Janes all ran versions on 20 August. The composition matters: NT$691.9 billion in the Ministry of National Defense budget, NT$218.2 billion in special budgets, NT$60.7 billion in non-profit special funds, plus NT$103.8 billion in military pensions and NT$47.9 billion for the Coast Guard Administration, on a NATO-style definition that President Lai has explicitly adopted. The headline is an 18 percent increase and the first time the figure has passed NT$1 trillion, with Lai targeting 5 percent of GDP by 2030. Two caveats a careless reader would miss. First, as a share of GDP the number falls, from 3.32 percent this year to 3.01 percent next year, because the overall budget rises 29.4 percent to NT$3.9266 trillion on the back of an AI-driven revenue surge and a NT$235.7 billion universal cash handout. Second, the budget still has to survive the opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan, which passed the 2026 budget only on 14 August after what CNA called a record 266-day delay (I note this corrects the 350-day figure carried in my prior write-up). So the defence build-out is real but not yet banked, and 21 August produced no Chinese response to it that I could find in Chinese Foreign Ministry, Taiwan Affairs Office or Global Times output.

The second dated item cuts the same way. On 19 August CNA reported that the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70 aircraft, tail numbers 6727 and 6728, departed the United States on 17 August Eastern time and are en route to Taiwan with air-to-air refuelling and a maintenance stop. The Peace Phoenix Soaring programme cost NT$247.2 billion between 2020 and 2026 and had slipped badly because of the production-line relocation and supply-chain disruption; Lockheed Martin has been running two shifts up to 20 hours a day. Delivery beginning is a genuine, if incremental, hardening of the target.

Third, on 20 August the Mainland Affairs Council released a poll conducted for it by National Chengchi University's Election Study Center between 13 and 17 August, n=1,086, margin of error plus or minus 2.97 points. Some 70.5 percent of respondents regard the Chinese coast guard patrols east of Taiwan as an act of ill will against 7.5 percent who see goodwill; 81.2 percent oppose one country, two systems; 83.6 percent favour maintaining the status quo; 83.9 percent say Taiwan's future should be decided by its 23 million people; 68.9 percent explicitly reject unification with the CCP. MAC notes the trend is stable. This is double-edged. It shows Beijing's maritime-legal accretion is generating hostility rather than acquiescence, which is an argument that the gray-zone track is failing and could eventually be abandoned for something harder; but it also shows that a blockade would face a population with no appetite for capitulation, which is the main reason blockades of this kind rarely deliver political results and are therefore rarely attempted. Also on 20 August the Central Election Commission fixed the nine-in-one local elections for 28 November 2026, with 11,051 offices and roughly 19.65 million eligible voters, pinning the date of the political failure point I have been tracking.

On the military tempo, the window is reassuring rather than alarming, and it revises my reading of the 19 August spike. Taiwan's MND, via its Political Warfare Bureau, logged 20 PLA aircraft sorties, 7 PLAN ships and 6 official ships in the 0600 18 August to 0600 19 August period, with 15 of the 20 entering the northern, central, southwestern and eastern ADIZ. I flagged that four-fold jump as noise on 19 August. It now has an explanation: MND issued a separate press release at 1310 on 18 August stating that from 0855 that morning it had detected 18 sorties of J-10, J-11, J-16 and KJ-500 aircraft, 13 of which penetrated the median line or its extension, coordinating with PLAN vessels under the pretext of a so-called joint combat readiness patrol. Per the GlobalSecurity archive of MND releases, that was the third such JCRP announcement in August alone, after 4 and 15 August. JCRPs are unnamed, short, recurring and have never converted into anything; a JCRP-driven one-day sortie count of 20 sits well inside a 2024-25 baseline that regularly exceeded 30. Nothing in the window resembles a warning indicator: no named exercise, no NOTAM or closure area, no mobilisation, no requisitioning of civilian roll-on/roll-off ferries, no reserve call-up. Taiwan's own Friday front pages, per CNA's 21 August headline roundup at 1019, are the 2027 budget (United Daily News, Liberty Times, Taipei Times), record July export orders of US$97.9 billion (Economic Daily News, Commercial Times) and a KMT unity event (China Times). When Taipei's press treats the strait as unremarkable, that is evidence.

Beijing's output in the window was rhetorical and united-front in character. On 19 August Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian welcomed Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim's statement that Taiwan is part of China and repeated that China must and will be reunified, and Global Times ran a companion piece claiming the DPP was rattled; also on 19 August a mainland spokesperson in People's Daily criticised the DPP for obstructing cross-strait exchanges. That is legitimacy work, not military signalling.

The one genuinely upward item consummates rather than extends the story I logged on 19 August. USNI News reported on 20 August that USS George Washington (CVN-73), with USS Robert Smalls (CG-62) and USS Shoup (DDG-86), arrived in the CENTCOM area of responsibility on 19 August after transiting the Arabian Sea, to relieve USS Abraham Lincoln, which has been deployed 272 days and gone 252 without a port call. USS Theodore Roosevelt is in San Diego after RIMPAC 2026, and no replacement carrier has been announced for the western Pacific. So the gap is now a fact, not a projection. I want to flag a trap I nearly fell into: a Newsweek piece headlined 'Oldest US Aircraft Carrier Fills Pacific Power Gap With China' surfaces in searches for this, but it is dated 24 March 2025 and concerns the Nimitz; it does not apply, and I am not treating the gap as filled. Even so, I weight this modestly. A carrier gap in Asia also occurred in 2024 without incident, an invasion requires months of observable preparation that has not begun, and the September summit calendar argues against action.

That calendar is intact. The White House and Secretary Rubio continue to confirm Xi's state visit to Washington on 24 September 2026, with Rubio framing the aim as another positive visit, notwithstanding Trump's July claims that China compromised 220 million voter files, which he himself downplayed within five days and which declassified intelligence undercut per Washington Post reporting of 30 July. Meanwhile the US$14 billion Taiwan arms package that Congress pre-approved in January 2026, reportedly including PAC-3 MSE and NASAMS, was still in administrative review as of 7 August, with Representative McCaul expecting notification soon and analysts expecting it only after the summit. Both capitals are managing to the same date.

Markets, pulled live from the Polymarket Gamma API at 08:27-08:31 UTC on 21 August: invasion by end-2026 sits at 3.8 percent Yes on US$39.88 million volume and US$584.8k liquidity; invasion by 30 September 2026 at 0.85 percent Yes on US$2.00 million; any China-Taiwan military clash before 2027 at 7.55 percent on US$3.23 million. The September market has softened from roughly 98.8 percent No on 12 August to 99.15 percent No. Manifold's ACX 2026 market on China attacking or blockading Taiwan during 2026 is 8.9 percent, and its 'attempt to invade by end of 2027' market 12.1 percent on 180k mana.

Why widen the upper bound. Two things I found today argue my right tail has been narrowing too fast. First, MetaculusBot mirrors on Manifold for the long-running 'full-scale blockade against Taiwan before the following years' series show roughly 41 percent for 2030 and 57 percent for 2035, versus 3.0 percent for the resolved 2025 sub-question. Those mirrors are thin (410 and 345 mana), probably stale, and the live Metaculus aggregate would not render for me, so I treat them as weak evidence. But they are a reminder that a blockade-inclusive question over 3.4 years is a materially different animal from an invasion-only one. Second, Badu and Mastro's East Asia Forum piece of 5 July 2026, which I read in full, argues that US munitions depletion from the Iran campaign, with more than half of the pre-war inventory of four key munitions expended and full Tomahawk replenishment possibly as late as 2030, plus Admiral Paparo's April 2026 testimony on shortfalls in amphibious ships, destroyers and attack submarines, may make the late 2020s look more favourable to Beijing than the present. That places a genuine window inside the back half of this question's horizon. Their countervailing point is stronger still on the assault limb: Xi's purges have removed more than 100 officers since 2022, including 41 of the 47 officers holding three-star rank in or after 2022, leaving the Central Military Commission with two active members after the January 2026 ousters of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli and six further removals in late June, with the Joint Staff Department hit hardest; the exercise record shows the strain, with Joint Sword organised in three to four days in 2024 against 19 days for Strait Thunder in April 2025. Their conclusion is that reconstituting command and control pushes the invasion timeline back further than US distraction pulls it forward, and that Beijing will prefer coercive maritime pressure and blockade rehearsals. That is a reallocation within my distribution rather than a change in its mass: less weight on assault, more on the blockade limb and on 2028-29 rather than 2026-27. Combined with the June 2026 precedent of Chinese coast guard vessels questioning commercial ships east of Taiwan and Taipei's July instruction that vessels refuse boarding demands, it justifies stopping the compression of the interval. Central estimate unchanged at 7; interval 4 to 11.
forecasts.base_rate:
Two reference classes anchor this forecast and both point to low single digits, with a third, softer source of evidence pointing higher and explaining why I keep a fat right tail.

The broad class is major-power initiation of an opposed amphibious assault, or a sustained naval blockade of a defended, populated territory, since 1945. Candidate cases are few: Inchon 1950 against a state already at war, Suez 1956, the Cuban quarantine of 1962 which was a partial interdiction lasting under a month, the Falklands in 1982 which was a British counter-invasion of a lightly garrisoned archipelago, the Iran-Iraq tanker war of 1984-88, and Russia's Black Sea grain interdiction from 2022. Across roughly 80 years and the small number of dyads possessing both the capability and a claimed casus belli, the annualised hazard for any given capable-power and target pair is on the order of 0.5 to 2 percent. Applied to the 3.36 years from 21 August 2026 to 1 January 2030, that yields roughly 2 to 7 percent. Blockade is by some distance the more available option than assault, which is why a question resolving on either sits above an invasion-only question. An opposed landing against an island of 23 million people across 130 kilometres of open water, with two narrow seasonal weather windows and a mountainous eastern coast, would be categorically harder than anything attempted since 1945.

The narrow, better-matched class is Taiwan Strait coercion episodes since 1995: the 1995 and 1996 missile crises; the August 2022 Pelosi encirclement exercises; Joint Sword 2024A in May 2024 and Joint Sword 2024B in October 2024; Strait Thunder 2025A in April 2025; and Justice Mission 2025 in late December 2025. Seven salient episodes in roughly 31 years. Every one was time-boxed to hours or days, announced or acknowledged as an exercise, and reversible. None involved boarding or interdiction of commercial shipping, a declared closure lasting beyond 72 hours, or escalation to assault. Zero for seven. A Laplace-style estimate of the per-episode conditional probability of conversion into a qualifying event gives roughly 1/(7+2), about 11 percent per episode. The 2026 opportunity rate is running below trend: SCMP reports PLA fighter sorties near Taiwan at a three-year low in the first half of 2026 and no large-scale named drill around the island in that period, the first such gap since 2022, with the coercion effort shifting from aerial missions toward coast guard patrols. Against 2 to 4 expected conversion opportunities across the remaining 3.36 years, that gives 4 to 9 percent. Below that sits a distinct, lower-frequency reference class of unannounced joint combat readiness patrols, of which MND publicly flagged three in August 2026 alone (4, 15 and 18 August); these are numerous, routine and have a conversion rate indistinguishable from zero, so they should not be counted as opportunities on the same footing.

Four adjustments. Upward, the PLA remains on the publicly reported trajectory toward being capable of a Taiwan operation by 2027 in successive US Department of Defense assessments, and its hardware base keeps growing: 12 submarines, a carrier, two cruisers, ten destroyers and seven frigates commissioned since 2024, 234 warships against the US Navy's 219, and a 2026 official defence budget up 7 percent to 1.91 trillion yuan. Upward, the PRC is building quarantine infrastructure that lowers the cost of the blockade limb specifically: China Coast Guard patrols east of Taiwan since 1 June 2026, the first-ever questioning of commercial vessels east of Taiwan in June 2026, Guangdong MSA Taiwan Strait traffic-control announcements, and survey and law-enforcement framing. Downward, the resolution bar is high and specific: a blockade exceeding 72 hours or an assault on Taiwan proper, confirmed by two major agencies. A quarantine framed as customs inspection, or a 48 to 72 hour encirclement exercise, both more likely than a true blockade, would probably not resolve YES. Downward, and newly weighted, Xi's purges have hollowed the command layer an invasion would need: more than 100 officers removed since 2022, 41 of 47 three-star officers, a Central Military Commission down to two active members, and the Joint Staff Department worst hit, with the exercise record showing 19 days to organise Strait Thunder in April 2025 against three to four days for Joint Sword in 2024.

The divergent evidence is the forecasting community's treatment of the blockade limb. Metaculus-mirrored markets imply something in the 30 to 41 percent range for a full-scale blockade before 2030, an order of magnitude above deep prediction markets on invasion (Polymarket at 3.8 percent for end-2026, 0.85 percent for 30 September 2026). Part of that gap is definitional: a loose blockade definition catches encirclement exercises that my resolution criteria would not. Part of it is staleness and thin liquidity in those mirrors. But I cannot fully dismiss it, and it is the main reason my interval runs to 11 rather than 10. Structural uncertainty remains high: the reference class is thin, the outcome turns on the private intentions of one decision-maker, and no historical frequency can capture that.
