forecasts.question: Will UK annual CPI inflation fall below 2.0% for at least one month before 1 January 2027?
forecasts.key_change: HOLD: 1 to 1, 80% interval unchanged at [0, 1]. Two days after the July print, the evidence arriving on 20 and 21 August 2026 has all pushed in the same direction as the print itself, and the practical floor for an integer forecast is where this question now sits. The structural point flagged in yesterday's reasoning is now verified against primary sources rather than inferred. The ONS release page for 'Consumer price inflation, UK: December 2026' carries a stated release date of 20 January 2027 at 7:00am and is marked 'not yet published', which puts the December reference month unambiguously outside the window. The ONS release pages confirm September 2026 data on 21 October 2026 and October 2026 data on 18 November 2026, and the August 2026 reference month is scheduled for 16 September 2026. November 2026 publishes in mid-December. So exactly four reference months remain publishable before 1 January 2027: August, September, October and November. Four attempts, no more. The arithmetic of those four attempts is now nailed down with the ONS's own index numbers rather than approximations. Table 1 of the July 2026 bulletin gives the CPI index (UK, 2015=100) as 139.0 for July 2025, 139.3 for August 2025, 139.3 for September 2025, 139.8 for October 2025, 139.5 for November 2025, and 142.9 for July 2026. A published annual rate 'below 2.0%' requires a printed 1.9% or lower, which needs a true ratio under roughly 1.0195. Working that through: August 2026 needs an index below about 142.0, September below about 142.0, October below about 142.5, and November below about 142.2. From 142.9 in July, that means the UK price level must fall by about 0.63% in a single month to catch August, by 0.63% cumulatively to catch September, by 0.26% cumulatively over three months to catch October, or by 0.47% cumulatively over four months to catch November. October is the softest target because October 2025 was itself a strong month (index up 0.4% month on month), but it is also the month in which the Ofgem cap resets upward. Every one of these paths requires an outright fall in the price level over a stretch that is seasonally positive, and the Bank of England's own central path implies the index rising to roughly 143.9 by November, about 1.2% above the level that would be needed. Nothing published in the last 48 hours narrows that gap; several things widen it. First, energy. Ofgem's assessment window for the October to December 2026 cap closed on 18 August 2026 and the confirmed level is due by 26 August. Cornwall Insight's August update, the most recent, forecasts a 4% rise to GBP 1,729 under Ofgem's revised typical-consumption definition, up from GBP 1,663 today, with the equivalent figure on the old definition GBP 1,941 against GBP 1,862. That is an upward revision in substance relative to the GBP 1,699.59 figure carried in yesterday's reasoning, and the wider analyst range being quoted ahead of the announcement is GBP 1,701 to GBP 1,747, all of it above the current level. Critically, the zero-rating of VAT on domestic electricity from 1 October 2026 is already netted into that number, so the single largest disinflationary policy event inside the window is not enough to stop the cap rising. On my own arithmetic, a 4% cap rise against an electricity-and-gas CPI weight of roughly four per cent adds on the order of 0.15 percentage points to the index in October alone, which is more than half the 0.26% fall that the October route to YES would require, and it moves the index in the wrong direction. Cornwall Insight's 19 August commentary also points to a further rise on 1 January 2027, which is outside the window for resolution but tells you where the wholesale curve sits. Second, the energy inputs themselves have hardened since the 19 August assessment. Brent traded around USD 92.69 on 20 to 21 August, up more than 4% on the week and up from roughly USD 87 in mid-August, on a US-Iran impasse and an unresolved confrontation over the Strait of Hormuz; President Trump said oil continues to flow but offered only that he would be open to resuming talks 'at some point'. UK gas has moved with it: NBP spot was around USD 19.80 and TTF spot around USD 20.55 in mid-August, both up close to 10%, with the NBP Winter-26 contract settling at 149.20 pence per therm on 11 August. Lower LNG inflows and subdued storage injections are pulling the same way. Third, the official and consensus forecast distribution has if anything tightened around a rising path. HM Treasury published 'Forecasts for the UK economy: August 2026' on 19 August 2026; the July edition of the same comparison had the independent average for Q4 2026 CPI at 3.4%, revised down from 3.7% in June, so even the direction of revision leaves the average some 1.5 percentage points above the threshold. The Bank of England's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report has CPI peaking at around 3.2% in 2026 Q4 with risks tilted to the upside, and an escalation scenario reaching as high as 4.5% by mid-2027. Deutsche Bank has 3.3% to 3.5% in Q4. No publicly identifiable institutional forecast has any month between August and November 2026 below 2.0%, and commentary continues to frame all forecasts as showing inflation above target for the whole of 2026. The Bank also projects annual food price inflation near 3.5% in December, a re-acceleration from the 1.3% recorded in July, which removes the one CPI division currently running well below target as a source of further disinflation. Fourth, the policy signal. A Reuters poll conducted 13 to 18 August found nearly 90% of economists expect Bank Rate held at 3.75% through the end of the year, and no economist expects a change on 17 September; markets on 16 August put roughly a one-in-four chance on a September hike and are pricing one quarter-point increase before year-end. KPMG's Yael Selfin expects a hold for the rest of the year, on the view that the Bank looks through energy-driven rises provided underlying pressures stay contained. A rate path with a hike priced and no cut is flatly inconsistent with sub-2% prints inside four months. Fifth, today's own data. ONS retail sales for July, released 21 August, fell 0.5% on the month, the first decline since April, with non-food volumes down 1.3% and clothing down 2.7%. That is genuine demand weakness and it is the strongest single item on the YES side of today's ledger. But it is partially offset by GfK consumer confidence for August, also published 21 August, at minus 14, a two-year high, up from minus 17 in July and well ahead of the minus 18 consensus. The two cancel to roughly nothing for the four-month price-level question. The upside channels that remain are unchanged and small. Grocery inflation at 2.1% in the four weeks to 9 August and CPI food at 1.3%, the lowest since September 2021, leave food a mild drag, but the Bank expects that to reverse. The labour market is loosening, with unemployment at 4.9% against 4.7% a year earlier, vacancies at 707,000 in May to July and regular pay growth at 3.5%, but 3.5% pay growth is consistent with services inflation near 3.4%, not with a sub-2% headline in 2026. The Autumn Budget is now confirmed for 28 October 2026, Chancellor John Healey's first, and this is the one place a large discretionary shock could still originate. But the timing is now clearly against it: a measure announced on 28 October would have to take effect within days to touch the November reference month, the last one that publishes in time. The government's own announced package points the other way on timing, with the GBP 2 bus fare cap in England starting January 2027, outside the window. That materially weakens the Budget as a route to YES relative to how it was weighted yesterday. Netting it all out, today's information is mildly negative for YES and does not justify a numerical move. The true probability is plausibly a few tenths of one per cent; 1 is the smallest positive integer available and correctly represents the residual mass sitting on a catastrophic energy-price collapse, an unannounced and very large fiscal intervention with an immediate effective date, or an ONS methodology or data incident. Holding at 1 with the interval at [0, 1].
forecasts.base_rate: The primary reference class is the historical frequency with which UK CPI annual inflation has printed below 2.0% within four months of a reading in the 2.7% to 3.1% band. Using ONS CPI back to 1989, months in that band number in the low hundreds, and the share followed within four months by a sub-2.0% print is on the order of 5% to 8%. That is the raw outside view and it is already low. It also overstates the case here for reasons that are structural rather than judgemental. The historical episodes delivering disinflation that fast were driven by sharp negative energy shocks or demand collapses: 2008 to 2009, when the financial crisis coincided with a temporary VAT cut; 2014 to 2015, when oil roughly halved; and 2020, when the pandemic plus VAT and hospitality measures compressed the index. The present shock is the opposite sign. Brent is near USD 92.69, up more than 4% on the week to 21 August 2026; NBP Winter-26 settled at 149.20 pence per therm on 11 August; and the administered-price calendar inside the window points up, with Cornwall Insight's August forecast of a 4% rise in the October cap to GBP 1,729 from GBP 1,663 and Ofgem due to confirm by 26 August. A second, much tighter and more informative reference class is the distribution of published forecasts for the specific months at issue. The Bank of England's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report has CPI peaking around 3.2% in 2026 Q4 with risks tilted to the upside and an escalation scenario reaching 4.5% by mid-2027. HM Treasury's July comparison of independent forecasters averaged 3.4% for Q4 2026, itself revised down from 3.7% in June; the August edition was published on 19 August 2026. Deutsche Bank has 3.3% to 3.5%. Not one publicly identifiable institutional forecast has any month from August to November 2026 below 2.0%. The standard deviation of one- to two-quarter-ahead UK CPI forecast errors is roughly 0.3 to 0.4 percentage points, wider during energy shocks. Asking for a single month to land below 1.95% from a central path of roughly 3.1% to 3.2% demands an error of about 1.2 percentage points in the disinflationary direction, three to four standard deviations. Even allowing for four correlated attempts and fat tails, that maps to well under 1%. A third and cruder class is the base rate at which the CPI index itself falls outright over a July-to-November stretch. Using the ONS's own Table 1 figures from the July 2026 bulletin, a sub-2.0% print now requires the index to fall from 142.9 in July 2026 to below roughly 142.0 by August or September, below roughly 142.5 by October, or below roughly 142.2 by November, that is cumulative falls of 0.26% to 0.63% depending on which month is targeted. In the inflation-targeting era since 1997, cumulative July-to-November falls of that size in the UK CPI index are confined to 2008-09 and 2020; the seasonal pattern over that span is mildly positive, and October 2025 alone rose 0.4% on the month. Combining the three classes, the outside view sits at roughly 0.5% to 2% before any inside-view adjustment, and every material inside-view adjustment cuts the same way: the cap rising on 1 October even after the electricity VAT zero-rating, oil and gas firm on the Hormuz impasse, core CPI stuck at 2.6% and core CPIH up to 2.9%, services at 3.4% with the softening attributed to an unwinding air-fares base effect, the Bank projecting food inflation back near 3.5% by December, and an MPC with a hike priced rather than a cut. The main limitation of these classes is that they capture discretionary policy poorly. The UK has twice in two decades used VAT to move CPI sharply, in December 2008 and July 2020, and the Burnham government has already zero-rated VAT on domestic electricity from 1 October 2026, worth about 0.10 percentage points. An intervention roughly ten times that size, with an effective date no later than November, would be needed. The Autumn Budget on 28 October 2026 is the only remaining vehicle, and its timing leaves at most one reference month to act on. That residual is what keeps the estimate at 1 rather than 0.

The residual risk structure is unchanged and, on the margin, slightly tighter than two days ago because the cushion has grown. Resolution requires the published worldwide cumulative on Box Office Mojo or The Numbers to exceed $1.5B at some point on or before 31 December 2026. That condition is already satisfied and has been continuously satisfied since roughly 13-14 August, when the film crossed $2B (Variety, Deadline and Forbes all published that milestone, with Deadline framing it as the second-fastest to $2B and Variety timing it at three weeks). The question does not require the figure to still stand above $1.5B on 31 December; it requires the gross to have exceeded $1.5B by that date, and a cumulative gross is monotonically non-decreasing under normal accounting. So the only paths to NO are (a) a catastrophic downward restatement of about $546M, or 26.7 percent of the published worldwide total, sustained through year end and reflected on both sources, or (b) a resolution-mechanics failure in which neither source is consultable or an adjudicator applies some perverse reading. Neither is live. On (a), major-studio worldwide cumes are compiled from Comscore domestic actuals and studio-reported international actuals; downward revisions do happen, but they run from hundreds of thousands to low single-digit millions and typically arise when a weekend estimate is trued up to actuals or a territory is reclassified. A half-billion-dollar haircut has no precedent for any wide release, still less for one whose milestones have been independently confirmed by three or four trade outlets. The redundancy in the resolution clause reinforces this: the question resolves YES on either source, so an error confined to one aggregator cannot flip it. That both sources agree to the dollar on all three lines today is itself weak positive evidence that the underlying feed is clean rather than one site carrying a stale or mis-keyed number.

On (b), nothing moved adversely. The Numbers resolved on the first attempt; Box Office Mojo resolved on the first attempt and, unlike two days ago, rendered its summary block without difficulty. Even if one aggregator went permanently dark, the other alone satisfies the resolution criterion. The trade record from Variety, Deadline, Forbes and Rotten Tomatoes' weekend column would survive the loss of both, so any reasonable adjudication has multiple independent fallbacks.

The forecast therefore stays at 100 with an 80% CI of [100, 100]. To be explicit about what that number means: 100 here is a rounding of a probability above 99.9%, not a claim of logical certainty. The skill's guidance against extreme probabilities absent extreme evidence is satisfied on its own terms, because the evidence is not a prediction but an observation - the outcome has already occurred, is published on both named resolution sources with a 36 percent margin over the threshold, and is cross-confirmed by independent trade reporting. Holding a meaningfully lower number would be a calibration failure in the opposite direction: paying a scoring penalty to hedge against an event class with zero observed instances. The honest residual is a few tenths of a percentage point covering resolver mechanics, wholesale re-audit scenarios and unmodelled pathways, and that residual is below the resolution of the integer scale the tracker uses. Continued daily monitoring now serves only to catch a resolution-mechanics anomaly; box office performance itself has been irrelevant to this question for well over a week, and will remain so.
forecasts.base_rate:
The naive reference class for this question is 'wide-release tentpole films that reach $1.5B worldwide'. That is a small set - fewer than fifteen titles in cinema history have crossed $1.5B - and the unconditional base rate for any given tentpole is low single digits. It was the correct frame in, say, June 2026, before release. It is the wrong frame now, and applying it today would be a textbook base-rate error of exactly the kind superforecasters are trained to avoid: selecting a reference class that discards the most informative conditioning information available.

The governing reference class today is 'published box office cumulative figures on a major aggregator that are subsequently restated below a milestone the film had already cleared'. The event has happened. Spider-Man: Brand New Day crossed $1.5B worldwide in roughly its second week of release, crossed $2B around 13-14 August, and stands at $2,046,432,089 on both named sources as of 21 August 2026. The forecasting question is no longer about future grosses. It is about whether an already-published, independently corroborated cumulative figure is revised downward by more than 26 percent and stays revised through 31 December 2026, on Box Office Mojo and The Numbers simultaneously.

I know of no instance of this. Aggregators do revise. The dominant mechanism is that studio-issued Sunday weekend estimates are replaced by Monday actuals, which historically move by roughly plus or minus one to three percent of the weekend figure, occasionally more for films with unusual preview or holiday patterns. Slower revisions occur when international territories are trued up against studio reporting, when a re-release is folded into or split out of a title's line, or when a distributor reclassifies which markets count as domestic. For a film a month past release, the magnitudes are almost always well under one percent of cume. The documented larger disputes in the historical record are of a different character: contested inflation-adjusted rankings, questions about reporting practice for certain local-language titles in China, and older films where the studio's own historical accounting was ambiguous. None involves a live 2026 Hollywood tentpole with Comscore-sourced domestic actuals, and none produced a downward restatement anywhere near 26 percent.

A second useful class is 'questions whose resolution condition is already met at the time of forecast, with an open window remaining'. For genuinely monotone quantities - cumulative gross, cumulative cases, cumulative funds raised - the historical resolution rate of such questions is effectively one hundred percent. The rare exceptions arise from ambiguity in the wording or from a resolver applying a different source than the one anticipated. Here the wording is clean, the threshold is a plain dollar figure, and the sources are named explicitly with an 'or' between them, which supplies redundancy rather than a conjunction of failure points. There is no snapshot subtlety: 'by 31 December 2026' sets a deadline for the event, not a test to be applied on that date. Even under the stricter snapshot reading, the answer is still YES, because cumulative gross does not fall.

A third relevant class is aggregator availability. Box Office Mojo, owned by IMDb and Amazon, and The Numbers, run by Nash Information Services, have each operated continuously for decades. Extended simultaneous unavailability through year end is a sub-0.1 percent proposition, and even that would not obviously produce a NO given corroborating trade reporting: Variety, Deadline and Forbes each published the $2B milestone in August 2026, and Deadline separately recorded the $1B international crossing as the second-fastest ever.

Combining these: the conditional base rate for NO, given an already-published cumulative 36 percent above threshold on two independent sources with matched figures to the dollar, is bounded above by the historical frequency of catastrophic aggregator restatements, which is zero over a large denominator of milestone crossings. A Laplace-style correction over a conservative denominator of several hundred modern-era milestone crossings gives an upper bound of a few tenths of one percent, and even that estimate is dominated not by restatement risk but by generic model uncertainty - the possibility that something about the resolution process, rather than the box office data, behaves unexpectedly. That is the whole of the residual, and it sits below the granularity of the integer scale this tracker reports on.

forecasts.question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change:
HOLD: 99 to 99. The 19-21 August window produced one genuinely new dated data point on the competitive split between the two companies and nothing at all that moves the combined run-rate arithmetic toward the $70bn bar. I ran a dozen distinct searches across Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, Reuters, The Information, CNBC, Axios, TechCrunch, Forbes and Fortune coverage plus company disclosures, and the standing verified figures are unchanged from yesterday. Dated items follow.

First, the anchor figures. Anthropic: revenue run rate above $65bn as at end-July 2026, reported by Bloomberg on 17 August (bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-17/anthropic-revenue-run-rate-surpasses-65-billion-ahead-of-ipo) and corroborated the same day by CNBC (cnbc.com/2026/08/17/anthropic-says-annualized-revenue-climbed-to-65-billion-in-july.html), Axios and TechCrunch. That is up from $47bn in May and roughly $9bn at end-2025. Anthropic's preliminary Q2 revenue was above $11.5bn (CNBC, 15 August), refined to $11.6bn with a $559m operating profit in the WSJ's 18 August piece, against $4.73bn in Q1 and $787m a year earlier. Second, OpenAI: annualised revenue run rate above $40bn, reported by Bloomberg on 13 August (bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-08-13/openai-s-revenue-run-rate-tops-40-billion-ahead-of-ipo) and repeated in Bloomberg's 14 August newsletter under the headline 'OpenAI Revenue Run Rate Tops $40 Billion, Doubling From 2025'. Supporting detail I confirmed today that I had not fully pinned down before: CFO Sarah Friar met investors on Friday 14 August and told them enterprise revenue now exceeds consumer revenue for the first time, that the enterprise line grew 20% in July alone, that business customer count grew 32% in July, and that the overall run rate was up 35% quarter to date with enterprise run rate up 50% quarter to date. OpenAI's Q2 recognised revenue was $6.7bn, up 18% sequentially from $5.7bn, with operating loss widening to $12.3bn from $9.3bn (WSJ, 18 August, corroborated by SiliconANGLE, Investing.com, Yahoo Finance and Outlook Business).

The arithmetic against the bar. On the exit run-rate reading that the word ARR in the resolution language most naturally points at, $65bn plus $40bn equals roughly $105bn against a $70bn threshold. That is a cushion of about $35bn, or 50% of the bar. For NO, the pair would have to shed a third of their combined run rate in the four months and ten days to 31 December, while both are inside live IPO processes, while enterprise adoption is still widening, and while every published monthly observation for either company in 2026 has been an increase. On the harsher reading, trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised, Q2 gives ($6.7bn + $11.6bn) times four, or $73.2bn, which still clears $70bn with about 4.5% headroom on data already six weeks stale. The question resolves on Q4, not Q2, and Q3 is running above Q2 for both firms on every reported indicator, so that headroom is widening rather than narrowing.

The one new item worth logging is TechCrunch, Julie Bort, published 20 August 2026 at 15:36 PDT, 'OpenAI is gaining on Anthropic with business users, new data indicates', which I fetched in full. It reports Ramp corporate-card data covering more than 70,000 US businesses. Anthropic took the lead in Ramp share in May at 41% to OpenAI's 39%; as of July Anthropic has nearly 44% to OpenAI's nearly 40%. Ramp economist Ara Kharazian says OpenAI is growing faster than Anthropic among this segment in Q3 to date, attributing it to GPT-5.6 Sol adoption among developers, and says Fable 5 'disappointed both in adoption and real-world application given price + data retention requirements'. Ramp declined to give dollar figures and the sample skews to tech. Crucially for this question, the same dataset shows the pie growing: the share of Ramp customers paying for AI at all passed 50% in March and reached nearly 56% by July. That is a share-rotation story between the two named companies, which is exactly the kind of news that leaves a sum unchanged, layered on top of a market-expansion story, which pushes the sum up. It is mildly net positive for the combined figure and I have logged it as such rather than as a change of view.

I also went looking specifically for disconfirming evidence in this window and found four things. One, TickerTrends (via Smartkarma and its own blog) publishes third-party ARR tracking that puts Anthropic at $74.1bn and OpenAI at $41.3bn in July, both above the company-sourced Bloomberg numbers, but argues Anthropic's month-on-month percentage growth has cooled from roughly 55% in the spring to mid-single digits by July. Deceleration in the growth rate is not contraction in the level, and mid-single-digit monthly growth from $65bn compounds to well over $80bn by December for Anthropic alone. Two, the gross-versus-net accounting dispute is now explicit and, importantly, quantified: OpenAI's own briefing to reporters puts the inflation from Anthropic's gross treatment of cloud-reseller end-customer spend at roughly $8bn, not at the punitive halving I stress-tested yesterday. Applying an $8bn haircut gives $57bn plus $40bn, or $97bn, still 39% above the bar. Three, the AI equity complex is under real pressure. CNBC on 18 August carried ECB economists warning that 'a correction of current stock market valuations is likely', and market wraps that day describe the S&P 500 falling for a third straight session as AI names sank. That is a valuation event, not a revenue event, and the transmission channel to booked enterprise contracts inside four months is weak. Four, the June 2026 precedent that the US government can pull a frontier model: I re-read Anthropic's own statement dated 12 June 2026 confirming that Commerce issued an export-control directive that forced Anthropic to disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for all users. That is the single best-evidenced tail risk in this question, because it is a demonstrated capability of the state rather than a hypothetical. It is also instructive on magnitude: Anthropic's run rate went from $47bn in May to above $65bn at end-July straight through that episode.

No public S-1 exists for either company as of 21 August; Anthropic's confidential draft went in on 1 June and OpenAI's on 8 June, with Anthropic targeting an October Nasdaq listing at a reported $2trn-plus valuation (Fortune and Forbes, 13 August) and OpenAI reportedly pushing to 2027. The FT's reported investor expectation that Anthropic finishes 2026 between $100bn and $120bn implies Anthropic clears the $70bn bar on its own. Nothing in the last 48 hours contradicts any of that. Residual probability continues to sit with resolver mechanics, a simultaneous restatement of both companies, and genuine catastrophic tails, which together I keep at about 1%. Holding at 99, interval 98 to 99.
forecasts.base_rate:
The governing reference class is not 'will two firms grow into a threshold' but 'a threshold is already exceeded on the public record with roughly 50% headroom four months before the measurement date; will it still be exceeded then'. That is a persistence question, and persistence questions of this structure resolve YES at very high rates. Across public forecasting platforms, questions whose resolution condition is already satisfied by a wide margin, in a domain with a monotonic underlying trend and no identified mechanism for reversal, resolve YES in the high nineties. The correct anchor is 97-99%, and the residual is dominated by resolution mechanics rather than by the world changing.

Three narrower classes point the same way. First, revenue trajectories of large private technology companies at $10bn-plus scale. Documented instances of a firm's disclosed annualised revenue falling more than 30% within two quarters, absent fraud or an exogenous demand collapse, are close to unrepresented. The available cases are Wirecard and FTX, where revenue was substantially fictitious, and the 2020 travel and hospitality shock, where the demand base physically disappeared. Neither template maps onto enterprise AI subscriptions and API consumption in H2 2026, where the observable direction of travel is budget expansion: Ramp's July 2026 cut shows the share of its 70,000-plus business customers paying for AI at all rising from just over 50% in March to nearly 56% in July. Base rate for a 33% two-quarter contraction here is well under 1%.

Second, the reporting-continuity class. Resolution requires credible outlets to publish a Q4 2026 figure for each company. Over the past eighteen months Bloomberg, The Information, the Wall Street Journal, CNBC, Reuters and the FT have each published multiple dated run-rate figures for both firms at a cadence of roughly one update every four to eight weeks per company; in August 2026 alone there are dated Bloomberg figures on the 13th for OpenAI and the 17th for Anthropic, a WSJ quarterly breakdown on the 18th, and a CNBC preliminary Q2 on the 15th. Two live IPO processes raise disclosure frequency rather than lowering it: a public S-1 must precede any roadshow by fifteen days, so if Anthropic lists in October, audited or reviewed figures enter the public record well before year end. The probability that no credible Q4 figure exists for either company is very low, and a resolver facing that case would fall back on the most recent available figures, which already clear the bar by 50%.

Third, the firm-specific trajectory class. Anthropic: roughly $9bn run rate at end-2025, $19bn in March, $30bn in April, $47bn in May, above $65bn at end-July, with Q1 revenue of $4.73bn and Q2 above $11.5bn. OpenAI: above $20bn at end-2025, a plateau near $25bn from February to May, then $40bn-plus by mid-August, with July alone adding more than 20% to the monthly run rate and enterprise customer count up 32% in that month. Every published observation in both series is an increase or a plateau. There is no observation of a decline from which to build a contraction base rate, which is itself a limitation of the class as much as a support for it.

The limitations are real and worth stating plainly. Run rate is not a governed accounting concept; it is a company-supplied annualisation of a short window, and the two firms compute it differently, a caveat Axios attached explicitly on 17 August and Forbes flagged as early as March 2026. Anthropic books cloud-reseller end-customer spend gross, and OpenAI has briefed that this inflates the reported gap by roughly $8bn. ASC 606 principal-agent guidance means contractual labels will not survive SEC review untested, so a net-basis restatement in a public S-1 is a live event, not a hypothetical. That makes the class of 'reported figures that survive an SEC review unchanged' thinner than the class of 'reported figures'. There is also a plateau precedent inside OpenAI's own series: roughly zero net run-rate added between February and May 2026, which shows these curves can flatten.

The restatement risk is bounded by arithmetic rather than judgement. Combined standing figure about $105bn. Apply OpenAI's own $8bn estimate of Anthropic's gross-basis inflation: $97bn. Apply a punitive halving of Anthropic's number: $72.5bn, still YES. Switch to trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised on Q2 data: $73.2bn, still YES. Only a simultaneous, severe restatement of both companies produces NO, and no source suggests anything of the kind.

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change:
HOLD: 32 to 32. The 19-21 August 2026 window delivered a dense run of UK data, but almost all of it is cyclical, and none of it moves the structural arithmetic that governs this question. Yesterday's cut from 34 to 32 already absorbed the one genuinely question-relevant release of the week - the ONS Productivity flash estimate and overview, UK: April to June 2026, published 18 August 2026, which showed RTI-based output per hour up only 0.7 per cent in the year to Q2 2026 (0.6 per cent adjusted for the LFS telephone collection error), down from 2.1 per cent in Q1, and the level falling from 5.5 to 4.6 per cent above the 2019 average, with the LFS-based measure outright negative at minus 0.2 per cent. Today's items sit either side of that and roughly cancel.

The headline new release is ONS Public sector finances, UK: July 2026, published this morning, 21 August 2026. Public sector net borrowing was 1.8 billion pounds in July, 0.7 billion pounds (68.7 per cent) higher than July 2025, against a consensus of roughly zero and an OBR March 2026 profile that implied a 0.5 billion pound surplus. Borrowing in the financial year to July stands at 56.7 billion pounds - 6 billion pounds lower than at the same point last year, helped by stronger receipts, but more than 2 billion pounds above the OBR path. Public sector net debt is 2.985 trillion pounds, 94.1 per cent of GDP. A record July for income tax receipts was not enough to offset spending and debt interest. Provenance note: I could not fetch the ONS July 2026 bulletin page directly (blocked by provenance restrictions), and the ONS 'latest' public sector finances page exceeded the fetch size limit, so these figures come from wire copy and trade press summaries of this morning's ONS release, including BM Magazine and the PA report carried by LBC, the North Wales Pioneer and the Stratford Herald.

Why this is worth only a fraction of a percentage point on a 2030s question: it pins down, rather than reveals, the shape of the 28 October 2026 Budget. Chancellor John Healey has confirmed that date and said his first fiscal statement will be 'built on fiscal discipline' and 'will meet our fiscal rules'. Independent estimates of the gap he must close cluster around 24 billion pounds by the end of the decade, and this would be Labour's third consecutive tax-raising Budget after the 41.5 billion pound package in 2024 and 26 billion pounds in November 2025. The 2030s channel runs through a higher structural tax burden on capital and labour, and through debt interest crowding out public capital spending. That channel is exactly what the OBR's Fiscal risks and sustainability report of 7 July 2026 describes: the projections start from the March 2026 medium-term forecast position in 2030-31, where a primary surplus of 1.5 per cent of GDP is planned, and show demographic and other pressures pushing a primary deficit back open during the 2030s. A 2 billion pound in-year overshoot does not change that trajectory; it makes the tax-raising Budget marginally more certain.

On rates, the 30-year gilt closed just over 5.61 per cent on 19 August 2026, reported as the highest level since 1998, on shifting expectations for Bank of England cuts. That is consistent with, and slightly below, the 5.7 per cent noted for 18 August in yesterday's write-up, so it confirms an elevated long-run real rate environment rather than signalling fresh deterioration. Elevated term premia remain a real 2030s headwind through the cost of capital and through the fiscal envelope for public investment, but the level is already in the forecast.

Two cyclical prints pull in opposite directions and net to roughly nothing. ONS Retail Sales, Great Britain: July 2026, also published 21 August 2026, showed volumes down 0.5 per cent on the month - the first fall since April - partly reversing a downwardly revised 0.7 per cent June rise, with sales excluding automotive fuel down 0.9 per cent and the annual rate slowing to 1.6 per cent from 3.8 per cent in June. Against that, GfK/NIQ consumer confidence for August 2026, released overnight on 20-21 August, rose to minus 14 from minus 17, a two-year high, beating a Reuters poll expectation of minus 18; the major-purchase sub-index reached its highest since December 2021, and economic expectations hit a two-year high, with commentary attributing the improvement partly to the new Burnham administration and easing energy prices. Confidence indices have close to zero predictive content for decade-ahead potential output, and a single month of retail volumes has less. The British Chambers of Commerce also published 'Businesses Continue to Feel the Inflationary Heat' on 19 August 2026, consistent with the 2.9 per cent July CPI print, and 'Economic Priorities for Government: Devolution' on 18 August - advocacy, not evidence.

I re-checked the structural anchors and none has moved. The OBR's March 2026 Economic and fiscal outlook still assumes trend productivity growth picking up to 1.0 per cent in the medium term, with labour supply growth falling to about 0.5 per cent by 2030, GDP growth of 1.1 per cent in 2026 and an average of 1.6 per cent over the remainder of the forecast. The IMF Executive Board concluded the 2026 Article IV consultation on 16 July 2026, putting 2026 growth at 1.0 per cent and describing the economy as having grown at its potential rate of 1.4 per cent in 2025, with growth stabilising around potential in the medium term. The Bank of England's framing, set out by Andrew Bailey in his May 2026 Cutlers' Feast speech, puts post-financial-crisis potential supply growth at about 1.3 per cent a year - 0.4 percentage points productivity plus 0.8 percentage points labour supply - against 2.8 per cent in 1990-2006. NIESR's trend estimate is 1.25 per cent. That cluster of 1.0 to 1.4 per cent is the single most important fact in this forecast, and the composition matters: the Bank's 1.3 per cent leans on 0.8 percentage points of labour supply that ONS demographics will not reproduce in the 2030s, when natural change turns negative and the working-age population grows at roughly 0.34 per cent a year.

On the AI channel, the evidence in this window remains suggestive rather than decisive. Bank of England analysis reported on 6 August 2026 found software and IT consulting firms increased their contribution to annual productivity growth tenfold versus the pre-Covid decade, to 0.1 percentage point in 2023-2025, with information-service providers flipping from drag to driver. A tenfold increase to 0.1 percentage point is an order of magnitude short of what is needed to close a 0.5 percentage point trend gap. Thomas Aubrey's decomposition for the Bennett School of Public Policy (8 June 2026) is a useful corrective: it shows the RTI-based gains concentrated in Information and Communication, Professional and Scientific and Financial Services, but attributes part of the Information and Communication contribution to a telecoms deflator that has fallen 21 per cent since 2019, and notes that imputed rent adds about 0.5 percentage points to measured whole-economy productivity growth over the period. Some of the apparent improvement is deflator methodology and accounting construct, not diffusion. EY's UK Economic Outlook of 3 August 2026 reinforces the narrowness: ICT plus professional, scientific and technical services accounted for 70 per cent of UK GDP growth between 2020 and 2026, while construction output per hour is broadly unchanged since 1997, and EY downgraded 2026 business investment to minus 0.7 per cent from zero.

Policy news in and around the window is mildly positive but small in magnitude: fiscal devolution announced on 31 July 2026, giving metro mayors a retained share of income tax and business rates from spring 2027 with detail deferred to the Budget; the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme, due to come into force in 2027, cutting electricity costs by up to 25 per cent for more than 7,000 electricity-intensive firms; and a 300 million pound National Wealth Fund-backed package announced in August 2026 for two data centres in the North Lanarkshire AI Growth Zone, contracted to CoreWeave on a 15-year lease. Each is plausible and each is an order of magnitude too small on its own to shift a decade trend by half a percentage point.

Net: a marginally worse fiscal print and a confirmed 27-year high in long gilt yields on one side; a two-year high in consumer confidence and continued AI-infrastructure commitment on the other. Nothing structural. Hold at 32 with the interval unchanged at 20-46.
forecasts.base_rate:
The natural reference class is UK decade averages of annual real GDP growth. On ONS data the arithmetic mean of annual growth rates was roughly 2.2 per cent in the 1990s, 1.8 per cent in the 2000s (dragged down by 2008-09), and about 2.0 per cent in the 2010s (flattered by recovery from a deep output gap). The 2020s to date average roughly 1.0 to 1.2 per cent. For 2026 the HM Treasury comparison of independent forecasts published in July 2026 gave an average of 1.0 per cent for both 2026 and 2027; EY's 3 August 2026 Outlook has 0.9 per cent for 2026 and 1.2 per cent for 2027; KPMG has 0.7 per cent; the IMF 1.0 per cent. Three of the last four completed or near-completed decades cleared 1.5 per cent, giving a naive base rate of 60 to 75 per cent. That base rate is heavily contaminated. The pre-2008 decades rested on roughly 2 per cent trend labour productivity growth plus sustained labour force expansion from rising female participation and, from the mid-2000s, EU accession migration. Neither condition holds now. The 2010s number is an output-gap artefact: it reflects reflation of a deeply depressed economy after 2009 rather than a 2 per cent supply-side trend, and productivity growth over that decade was roughly 0.5 per cent a year.

A better-matched class is the post-2008 UK trend. On the ONS productivity flash of 18 August 2026, output per hour on the RTI-based measure is 4.6 per cent above the 2019 average as of Q2 2026 - about 0.64 per cent a year over seven years - while the LFS measure is 2.3 per cent above, about 0.32 per cent a year. Whole-economy GVA is 7.1 per cent above its 2019 average, roughly 1.0 per cent a year of realised GDP growth over 2019-2026. That last figure is a direct ONS-sourced read on the exact quantity this question asks about, and it sits a third below the resolution bar. If the 2030s look like the post-2008 UK, the decade average lands near 1.0 to 1.2 per cent and the question resolves NO.

A third class is official and quasi-official estimates of current potential growth, which is the closest thing to a forecast of the 2030s starting point. These cluster tightly: the OBR's March 2026 EFO assumes medium-term trend productivity growth of 1.0 per cent, below the 1998-2007 average of 2.1 per cent but above the 2010-2019 average of 0.6 per cent, with labour supply growth falling to about 0.5 per cent by 2030 and GDP growth averaging 1.6 per cent over the forecast after 1.1 per cent in 2026. The IMF's 2026 Article IV, concluded 16 July 2026, puts UK potential at about 1.4 per cent. Andrew Bailey's May 2026 speech puts realised post-crisis potential supply growth at 1.3 per cent a year, decomposed as 0.4 percentage points productivity and 0.8 percentage points labour supply, against 2.8 per cent in 1990-2006. NIESR's trend estimate is 1.25 per cent. Not one of these anchors sits above 1.5 per cent, and the Bank's decomposition is the most instructive: the labour-supply component that did most of the work post-crisis is precisely the component demographics will withdraw in the 2030s.

A fourth class is decadal growth forecasts for advanced economies made three to four years ahead of the decade start. These have been poorly calibrated in both directions: the 2010s were widely under-forecast at the trough of the crisis, the 2020s were over-forecast pre-COVID, and long-horizon OBR and Bank potential-growth assumptions have repeatedly been revised down over the past fifteen years. The revision asymmetry is real - the OBR has cut its trend productivity assumption several times and has essentially never raised it materially - which argues for weighting the pessimistic tail more heavily than a symmetric distribution around a 1.2 per cent central case would.

The demographic accounting is the tightest constraint. The ONS 2024-based National Population Projections (published 28 April 2026) put the working-age population up 1.5 million, or 3.4 per cent, between mid-2024 and mid-2034 - about 0.34 per cent a year - with natural change turning negative from around mid-2026 onwards, so that beyond the mid-2030s population growth is entirely migration-dependent. With hours per worker on a mild downward trend and the employment rate at best flat given ageing, labour input plausibly contributes 0.0 to 0.4 percentage points a year in the 2030s. To average above 1.5 per cent you therefore need trend productivity growth of roughly 1.1 to 1.5 per cent a year sustained for a decade - comfortably above the OBR's 1.0 per cent assumption and roughly double the realised post-2019 rate on ONS's preferred measure.

Two mechanical considerations push up. First, an output-gap effect: if the UK has a recession in the late 2020s, the 2030s decade average is mechanically boosted by recovery growth, as the 2010s were. With unemployment at 5.0 per cent, that path is far from remote. Second, ONS revisions have skewed upward for post-pandemic UK GDP, and the question resolves on ONS-reported figures. Blending a base-rate-consistent central of about 1.15 per cent with a standard deviation of roughly 0.45 percentage points across the plausible decade-average distribution, and adding weight for the recession-recovery and revision channels, gives a probability in the low thirties.

key_uncertainties: Whether AI diffusion delivers economy-wide measured productivity gains in the 2030s or stays concentrated in ICT GVA and data-centre capex - the Bank of England's 0.1pp contribution from software and IT consulting is real but two orders of magnitude short of closing the gap
Which productivity series is right - RTI (output per hour 4.6% above 2019) or LFS (2.3% above) - and what the new ONS component-based method and the autumn 2026 RTI-LFS-TLFS linkage findings conclude
How much of the recent measured improvement is deflator and imputed-rent artefact rather than genuine diffusion, as Aubrey's Bennett School decomposition implies

Net migration policy through the 2030s: with natural change negative from around mid-2026, labour force growth is almost entirely a policy variable, and a swing from 100k to 400k a year is worth roughly 0.3-0.5pp of annual GDP growth

Whether a recession occurs before 2030 - the Strait of Hormuz scenario in EY's August 2026 Outlook implies a 0.2% contraction in 2027 - which would depress the late 2020s but mechanically lift the 2030s decade average

The path of long-run real interest rates and the fiscal envelope: with debt at 94.1% of GDP and 30-year gilts near 27-year highs, whether debt interest forces sustained cuts to public investment through the 2030s
Whether the 2028-29 general election produces a government that sustains or reverses the current supply-side agenda (planning, fiscal devolution, industrial electricity costs, AI infrastructure)
Statistical resolution risk: how ONS methodology changes, Blue Book revisions and any base-year rebasing shift the reported 2030-2039 annual growth rates relative to first estimates
